speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in view of the concern expressed during current hearings of the United States federal power commission over the fact that the permit issued under our Electricity and Fluid Exportation Act for the export of natural gas from the Peace river area to the northwest United States is for one year only, has the government given consideration to enacting a regulation making it possible to grant a permit for this particular export which will be in effect over a period of years rather than on the present year to year basis? The Minister of Trade and Commerce will realize the great importance of this project to British Columbia.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: IS, 1953 QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS IMPORTS FROM UNITED KINGDOM BY FEDERAL GOVERNMENT
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED INCREASE IN TERM OF PERMIT FOR EXPORT OF GAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend was good enough to give me notice of his question. The house will recall that on March 13 I dealt at some length with the government's policy with respect to the export of oil and gas. In the course of my remarks I pointed out that the government had issued an export licence to Westcoast Transmission Company Limited for the export of natural gas. The licence as issued was to be renewable from year to year, and the Canadian government was prepared to accept responsibility for providing gas in quantities as specified in the licence for the full period of the existing permit issued by the province of Alberta. This was of course contingent upon Westcoast meeting its obligations to supply customers in British Columbia.
Hon. members will be aware that the principal considerations in the construction and operation of any gas pipe line are that sufficient gas must be transported for such periods as will permit the amortization of the capital costs of construction; that adequate and continuing deliveries of gas must be assured to distributors to enable them to underwrite the capital costs of distribution; that adequate and continuing supplies of gas must be assured to consumers. Having
3882	HOUSE OF
Inquiries of the Ministry regard to these and other considerations, it now appears desirable to crystallize the undertaking given with the licence already issued to Westcoast. The government has therefore issued an amended licence to West-coast Transmission Company Limited for a period of twenty-two years for the export of surplus gas, the volumes to be determined from time to time by the Canadian government but to be not less than the quantities specified in the permit. In so doing, the requirements of British Columbia will of course be protected.
Bearing in mind that without export the construction of this line would be postponed perhaps for all time, the government in reaching this decision also recognizes the unanimous resolution passed by the province of British Columbia endorsing this project, and the permit issued by the province of Alberta for twenty-two years, as well as the dedication by that province of the Peace river gas to this project. To enable the government to issue such a licence, it has been necessary to amend the regulations under the Electricity and Fluid Exportation Act, and this has been done. This amendment provides that in the case of export of surplus natural gas the period of the export licence shall be determined by the governor in council. Export licences for electricity and petroleum remain, as before, on a yearly basis.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Digby-Yarmouth (Mr. Kirk) asked me if I would make a statement on the position of the Bar Harbor-Yarmouth ferry. I am pleased to do so now.
On November 7, 1952, authority was given for entry into a contract with the Davie Shipbuilding and Repairing Company Limited of Montreal, for the construction of an automobile ferry between Yarmouth, N.S., and Bar Harbor, Maine. The specification called for delivery of the vessel within eighteen months from date of contract, as well as engines which would guarantee a service speed of 18 J knots.
Deliberations began immediately between the technical officers of that company, the naval architect and officers of this department.
It became evident that the specification, which had been prepared by the naval architect, did not provide for sufficient power to allow the proposed vessel to operate on a service speed of 18J knots. This fact, plus some doubts expressed by the contractor as to the stability of the vessel as designed, made it necessary that tank tests be per-

The tank tests were performed in England and the United States, and the results substantiated the contention of the shipyard as to the two points mentioned above. This has, therefore, brought about some redesigning and alterations in the ship as originally designed, which the shipyard has been authorized to perform.
Davie Shipbuilding and Repairing Company guarantee that the vessel will be delivered eighteen months after contract is signed. This means that the ship will still be delivered in 1954, but unfortunately it appears doubtful that it will be economically feasible to begin operation in late 1954. It would be preferable to delay the opening of the service to the summer months of 1955, when traffic would be available in sufficient volume to allow the economic operation of the service.

My reason for raising this now, rather than on the orders of the day where I might have done it, is that it would have taken me a little longer than is permitted at that stage of our proceedings.
I have had brought to my attention by a person in Montreal something which rather amazes me. Indeed when this correspondent first wrote to me about the matter I could hardly believe what he told me and I asked him to submit the evidence to which he had referred. I have now received this evidence in the form of a bill from the Montreal General Hospital and I should like to draw it to the attention of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) and have his comment on it.

This is a bill, as I have already said, from the Montreal General Hospital, account No. C93951, under date of March 23, 1953, and the total amount of the bill happens to be $70.61. One item on it is for medicine, $5.10, and further along in the same line where "medicine" is printed, are the words
fMr. Chevrier.]

It has been my understanding from the law, from debates in this house, and from my own unfortunate experiences in having to pay hospital bills, that medicines supplied to hospitals are not subject to federal taxes. I assume in this case that the reference is to the sales tax. I have in my hand, as a matter of fact, another hospital bill and this one comes from Manitoba. When I look into the legislation in connection with this matter, namely the Excise Tax Act, I find that articles and materials for the sole use of any bona fide public hospital, certified to be such by the Department of National Health and Welfare, when purchased in good faith and for use by the hospital and not for resale, are exempt from the sales tax.

speechtext:
There is one matter I should like to raise before you leave the chair, Mr. Speaker. It has been raised on other occasions in the house. It has to do with the grain handlers' strike in Vancouver, which has continued on and on during the weeks, with deteriorating effects upon the marketing of wheat. As I understand it, within the last couple of days, the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) has received a telegram from the president of the Saskatchewan farmers' union in reference to this matter. Reports have been made almost from day to day by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg), but apparently the situation in Vancouver is no nearer solution than it was weeks ago.
While the delay in settlement continues, the serious situation with respect to marketing is being continued and intensified. I hold in my hand a copy of a telegram that was sent to the Prime Minister by Mr. Phelps, the president of the Saskatchewan farmers' union, and I bring it to the attention of the house as the views expressed by the provincial board of the Saskatchewan farmers' union now in session in Saskatoon. The telegram was sent to the Prime Minister on April 14 and reads in part as follows:
Provincial board Saskatchewan farmers' union meeting special session appreciate government's efforts resolve dispute Vancouver terminal elevators. Farmers increasing concern its continuation if further efforts along lines previously pursued fail in accomplishment . . .
The government is requested to take certain drastic courses by the union, or in any event-
-to request the prairie farm unions to negotiate settlement immediately between companies and union which we are prepared . . .
That is, to consider settlement. The strike has continued for a very long time. Much has been said of the success attained in the settlement of the impending railway strike a few months ago. This is one that affects the farmers of the western provinces to a degree that few of us really appreciate, and it has exercised the minds of farmers throughout the west to a degree that I have not seen in a considerable period of time. I would appreciate it very much if the Prime Minister would say what his reaction is to the representations that have been made, the last one by the farmers' union, and also whether he is in a position, as leader of the government, to hold out any hope of an
Certainly no one can say that an endeavour has not been made by the representatives of the Department of Labour to achieve something in the nature of a settlement of this matter. However one suggestion that has been made-and I repeat it-is that the representatives of the companies and the workers be brought to Ottawa in order to discuss the matter with the Prime Minister and the Minister of Labour. I believe that bringing them face to face with the cabinet, in the same way as was done in the other matter of recent days, could not but have beneficial results. For some reason the attitude of the Minister of Labour has been that such a course would not hold out any hope of beneficial results. Something must be done. The situation becomes more serious day by day. To follow such a course would result in neither side having to make any retreat from its position, but it would give the Prime Minister and the Minister of Labour an opportunity, in a face to face discussion with the representatives of the companies and of the workingmen, to achieve a measure of conciliation and compromise without which this matter will not be settled. The longer it takes, the more dangerous it is going to be and the more difficult of settlement. I suggest that the Prime Minister use his offices in that regard.
I suggest that the Prime Minister use his offices to bring these two jarring elements together and thereby do something definite to settle a matter which is becoming more insoluble as the days go on. All of us know that without the opportunity of conciliation being available, in the manner it would be should these people foe brought into consultation with the Prime Minister and the Minister of Labour, the more difficult it is going to be. I suggest that the farmers in western Canada do expect something in the nature of action such as that in order to achieve a settlement at the earliest possible date.

Unfortunately I do not know personally either the owners of these elevators or the leaders of the union, and I must confess that I know very little about the operation of elevators. I do know that it is a relatively small group of elevators that are involved in the strike and that whatever settlement is made is apt to affect not only these three or four or five elevators but also the whole industry all over the country. That
Strike of Grain Handlers is something which requires to be handled with tact.
All I can say is that no government would be discharging its responsibility if it allowed these essential implements of the grain trade to remain indefinitely out of service. Therefore I think that one must exhaust all possibilities of getting the parties to reach an agreement before looking upon it as a case where expropriation proceedings, or the equivalent thereof, are justified.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I venture to make a comment on this matter only because I find myself greatly surprised at the reason which the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) gave, namely that if the parties were asked to come here they would come without authority. It is very difficult for me to believe that if responsible people were asked to come to Ottawa by the government of Canada to discuss a matter they would venture to come and then say that they had no authority to represent the parties.
In the second place, the Prime Minister gave another reason which surprised me even more. He said that in the case of the railways he knew the parties concerned personally and in this case he did not. I venture to say with deference that surely that could have nothing to do with it. The parties will know well enough who the Prime Minister is. Having regard to the fact that sixty days have elapsed and also the urgency of the problem as indicated by members from Saskatchewan, frankly I feel that the reasons the Prime Minister has given are unconvincing.

maintopic: STRIKE OF GRAIN HANDLERS AT VANCOUVER

Mr. Speaker, I should like to add a word in support of the request that some further action be taken at this time. I was a bit disappointed with the remarks the Prime Minister made, but taking his own argument I should think that there is a real reason why he should intervene now. I would also think that the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) would have a very direct interest in the matter because he is the minister of the government responsible for these elevators and the marketing of grain. With the many weeks that have gone by, the situation has become very embarrassing and is causing considerable loss to western farm producers. While recognizing that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) and his officials have done a great deal toward trying to bring about a settlement, I think that the Prime Minister should now invite

Supply-National Defence the heads of the grain companies and the heads of the labour unions to come here. He and the Minister of Trade and Commerce should take a hand with the Minister of Labour to bring about a proper settlement in the interests of the producers who are being so embarrassed at this time. I would think these ministers should be vitally concerned about the matter and I hope that some action will be taken in the immediate future.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, last evening when the house rose I was discussing certain matters of interest arising from the general presentation of the Minister of National Defence yesterday and pointing out the difficulty that a private member faces in obtaining information on this important subject. As a result my discussion will largely take the form of questions and queries.
I was reviewing some of the attempts that I have made thus far to obtain information with respect to welfare services for the troops, a matter that interests me as well as other members of the house. On November 27 last I placed on the order paper a question to which I received a rather blunt and peremptory reply. I pursued the matter in another question asking for further details. The question I submitted on February 5 read as follows:
1.	What welfare service is now being provided at unit level for troops serving (a) in Korea, (b) in Germany?
2.	What staff at unit level is detailed exclusively to welfare service duty (a) in Korea, (b) in Germany?
3.	What voluntary welfare organizations are serving (a) in Korea (b) in Germany? How many personnel are involved?
4.	What Canadian amenities e.g. movies, news, comforts, etc., are available to Canadian forces abroad and how are these distributed?
That question was passed as an order for return and the return has not yet been brought down in the house, so I am still very much in the dark.
In a final effort I attempted to have the documents relating to this subject tabled, and that request was turned down. Therefore, I want to pursue this matter because, in spite of the fact that the minister has expressed the viewpoint that to resort to voluntary welfare services would be uneconomical, unnecessary and unwise, I still feel that there is considerable interest in this subject. That interest is displayed in recent reports from the organizations most concerned.
I was going to quote last evening from an article in the January issue of the Legionary, the official organ of the Canadian Legion in Canada. The Legion had directed a letter to the minister asking for information concerning the present attitude of the govern-

ment towards welfare problems. One or two excerpts from the minister's reply are interesting:
At present we have a brigade group in Korea, a reinforcement group and other units in Japan, an air force wing and a depot in England, a brigade in Germany and an air force wing in France.
The heads of the three services consider that it would be unwise, uneconomical and unnecessary to establish at all these places the five welfare agencies (Canadian Legion, Y.M.C.A., Salvation Army, Knights of Columbus, Red Cross) that we used during the second world war and I agree with them.
Now, that is substantially the same reply, only much briefer, that I received to my question on November 27. Another excerpt from the minister's reply is interesting:
From what I have seen and from the advice given to me by those whose responsibility it is, the conditions of service, general amenities and welfare services of the Canadians today are, having regard to the situation they are in, in every way as good and in most ways better than during the second world war.
That is rather an aspersion on the type of service that was offered by the voluntary organizations during world war I and world war II. From my knowledge of their activities, I think it would be pretty hard to supply the type of welfare services that those organizations provided during world war II; and I would doubt very much if what pertains to units serving abroad is equal in every respect today to the type of service which we who served in world war II were privileged to enjoy.
I come to another section of the reply:
As far as the 27th brigade is concerned, the same is true, but they are located in the neighbourhood of Hanover, a large city, with of course all the opportunities for religious worship, entertainment and sightseeing that a large city offers.
The implication there is to the effect that because the 27th brigade is located in a large urban area it would be possible for them to enjoy the social amenities extended to the German civilian population. However, recent reports from the well-known journalist, Bill Boss, would indicate that the situation is just the reverse-and that one of the major problems in Hanover is the inability of the troops to fraternize with the civilian population. The troops are regarded rather coldly and the explanation, as I have read it in these interesting dispatches, is that the residents of Hanover are rather standoffish people who do not easily extend hospitality to strangers in their midst. That, of course, may be a carryover from the situation that prevailed during world war II, but definitely according to reliable press dispatches-and unfortunately we have to depend on press dispatches in these matters as we are not able to determine from official
Supply-National Defence sources-the situation with respect to the 27th brigade has not been realized as it was anticipated in the reply to the Canadian Legion by the minister.
Now, I will move along to the Y.M.C.A.'s interest in this matter. There was a press dispatch in the Globe and Mail of February 27, 1953, reading as follows:
The Y.M.C.A. will press the government to do something about lack of recreational facilities in the army, both in Canada and overseas, when the annual national council meets today at the Royal York hotel.
A report to be tabled announces that the "Y" is already working with leaders of the Salvation Army, Y.W.C.A., the Canadian Legion, and the Knights of Columbus on a combined submission to be sent to Ottawa.
I presume that submission is already in the hands of the Department of National Defence.
That joint action gets around a difficulty that was outlined in the reply to my question of November 27, to the effect that it would not be possible to establish representatives of all these organizations with any one particular unit. Of course the experience of world war II should have provided the solution for that particular problem because, as I recall, only one representative of one particular organization serviced any one unit, whether it was army, air force or navy. In other words, the organizations pooled their resources and, in so doing, were able to provide a much more comprehensive and efficient welfare program.
I note that in so far as the Salvation Army auxiliary services are concerned they have taken the initiative and have voluntarily sent a team-I think it is a husband and wife team-to the Hanover area to work among the troops of the 27th brigade. I believe that was done at no cost or at very little cost to the Department of National Defence-which would remove the charge that the service would be uneconomical.
I do not want to labour this, but the main point I want to bring out is that it seems to me that there has been a trend toward militarization of welfare services-that is the incorporation of the welfare services within the body of the service units. I think that is contrary to the real spirit of welfare. Military organization, by its very nature, must have discipline and must have a certain rigidity in its functions. I cannot see that we can provide the subtleties necessary in meeting the welfare problems of servicemen by employing men in the forces who have been trained for military duties and not welfare duties.
There is another matter that must be kept in mind in regard to this welfare problem.

Supply-National Defence Our forces have always been, and I suppose they always will be-so long as we retain a democratic system-civilian, forces made up of personnel whose interests lie predominantly in the direction of civilian activities. It seems to me that the voluntary organizations have built up a vast reservoir of experience, during world war II in particular. I have been reading the story of the Y.M.C.A. in the war, and they built up tremendous resources in regard to the handling of service welfare problems, which, combined with their civilian capacity to serve, makes it almost inevitable that our own military organizations will have to depend upon that organization along with Others for meeting the welfare needs. The welfare problem is not only one that pertains to troops in the field or air personnel who are 6n active service. There is also a large area of welfare problems created, particularly when great numbers of civilians are called up and find it necessary to serve in foreign theatres. This precipitates a crisis in the families back home. We are well aware that divorce statistics went up during world war II and immediately following world war II. It is perhaps significant that divorces are again on the increase, following a decline during the years 1949, 1950 and 1951.
A good many of the men serving in the forces are married men with family responsibilities. They are removed from those responsibilities, and automatically social welfare problems are created which no military welfare set-up can handle. The representatives of the voluntary organizations serving in the field have immediate call upon the welfare resources of the organizations at home. The Y.M.C.A., in particular, has a unit in almost every major community in Canada, as has the Salvation Army. They are able to direct their personnel serving on the home front to give assistance in cases where domestic difficulties arise as a result of the absence of the husband and father from the home. I would suggest, Mr. Chairman, that no democratic military force can afford to dispense with the offer of service that has been so generously and so promptly put forward by each of these voluntary organizations.
There is one more aspect of the civilian question that I should like to mention. During world war II, auxiliary officers representing the voluntary organizations retained their civilian status. I saw them in action with my own squadron in the field, and with other units, and I thought such a condition was a decided advantage. In spite of the fact that the process of democratization has gone on in our military forces, there is still, a wide gap between the enlisted private or airman IMr. Dinsdale.l

and the officer. I know in my own squadron experience we lived apart in rather comfortable mess conditions, while the airmen took whatever was available. Even the problem of geographical separation, particularly while we were on the continent, was one of some proportions. The only time we were in touch with the men who serviced the aircraft, and the other airmen who were responsible for carrying on all the functions that are necessary to keep the aircraft flying, was when we met these men at the point of duty. It was the efforts of our welfare officer in organizing various entertainment activities and recreational activities that brought the officers and men together and created a much better situation so far as morale was concerned.
I believe that the very fact that a man is wearing pips or rings is a deterrent to coming to close grips with the intimate personal needs of the men who are serving in our armed forces. There is a line of social distinction that exists. Obviously the welfare officer, even if he had specialized social service training, is under a handicap in dealing with the men because of the fact he is wearing pips or rings. The soldier or airman in difficulty thinks twice before he bares his soul to such an individual. One of the advantages of using the voluntary organizations was the fact that the representative retained his civilian status, and the organizations provided excellent co-ordination between the commanding officer, the padre and the men. In addition to this they were always in direct contact with the domestic situation on the home front.
When the minister says the use of these services at the present stage of development of our armed forces is uneconomical, unnecessary and unwise, I would disagree most heartily with that statement. If we are moving towards the militarization of welfare,
I believe that the words which have been used to describe the use of voluntary systems might be more aptly applied to a strictly military program of welfare. Such a program is uneconomical because we can use our military personnel to much better advantage. It is unnecessary because we have social welfare agencies willing to undertake the job, and axiomatically such a program would be unwise.
I notice the minister says that the advice from the heads of the three services, the navy, army and air force, was against the use of these voluntary bodies. I can understand that problem. As civilians, auxiliary officers would not come under strict military discipline. They might constitute a thorn in the flesh, particularly when they are dealing with subtle, intimate personal problems, and they

might have a solution other than the prescribed military solution according to Q.R. (Air) or army regulations. Other disadvantages arise from the policy of maintaining strict military discipline over these auxiliary personnel, but they are more than compensated for by the fact that qualified and experienced welfare officers are able to get to the heart of the matter, are able to get under the surface and look at the problem from the standpoint of the real needs. The fact that the welfare bodies are continuing their representations and are compromising in every way to make it possible for them to serve the present defence needs, which has been stressed by the minister as an urgent and imminent one, is an indication of their willingness and interest in this matter.
I am going to leave the problem of welfare. It might be that, since the Y.M.C.A. and other organizations have made their representations, there has been a change in the interpretation of this problem. Unfortunately, we have not heard about it in the house. I have not been able to get any information from the various attempts I have made.
I now want to discuss briefly a statement that appears in the white paper on Canada's defence program. It is contained on page 5, section 13, subparagraph 1, which reads as follows:
The immediate defence of Canada and North America from direct attack;
That is given as the No. 1 priority under the objective of out defence policy, and according to the white paper that defence policy has remained unchanged since the reorganization of the services to meet the Korean crisis.
Then, going down to section 18 on page 5, we find that the defence department is moving to fill the gap, that has become increasingly evident so far as home defence is concerned, as follows:
Regular and reserve fighter squadrons, the backbone of the air defence network, are being built up. The first regular squadron, equipped with CF-100 all-weather, twin-engine jet fighters, was recently formed and by the end of the fiscal year a number of these squadrons will be operating. Meanwhile, a number of squadrons of F-86E Sabres, destined as part of Canada's NATO air contribution have been in Canada available for the defence of this continent. As the last of these are sent to Europe during the year, their places will be taken by squadrons of CF-100's. Reserve squadrons now equipped with Vampires and Mustangs will be re-equipped with CF-100's as these become available.
Ever since I came into the house hon. members on this side have been stressing the fact that priority No. 1 has been ignored in the build-up of Canada's defence. I agree heartily with the hon. member for Nanaimo. I remember when he was rather severely castigated because he dared to infer that
Supply-National Defence priority was not being given to the defence of this continent; but it becomes increasingly obvious that such is the case.
It is now generally recognized that Canada occupies a unique position with regard to air defence. The very fact that we are contributing to it at least half of the national defence budget indicates an emphasis in that direction. From the standpoint of military strategy, we guard the northern approach to the most vulnerable country of the western world, namely the United States of America; and therefore we have a special obligation, along with that country, to see to it that our home defences are adequate to meet any threat of attack. Then during our short military history, beginning with world war I and our participation in the Royal Flying Corps and again in world war II, Canadians have demonstrated that they have a special aptitude with regard to air warfare and air defence.
We of the official opposition gave emphasis to that viewpoint, during the discussion that arose from the appointment of an associate minister of national defence, when we suggested that it would be a more feasible plan to appoint a deputy minister for air who could concentrate exclusively on the important and highly necessary task of building up our defences for air. I do not know just how the defence department is organized, but recently in the Winnipeg Free Press a series of interesting articles attracted my attention. These articles proposed a much more logical, coherent and rational defence organization where the responsibility for policy determination would be removed from the shoulders of the heads of the departments and would be placed in the hands of some sort of military council which would be in a position to deal more adequately with the difficult problems that are connected with our defence build-up.
The suggestion that we appoint a special deputy minister for air was turned down and we are carrying on much in the same hit-or-miss fashion that has been going on in the past few years.
To come directly to this matter of defence for Canada, we have had it brought to our attention forcibly by certain air force personnel that, so far as air defence is concerned, we are wholly inadequate in this regard. Wing Commander Rohmer in Toronto, towards the end of March, made a statement in this regard.

That is notwithstanding the fact that we had to start from scratch. We


had no previous experience in this regard. But I do agree with this criticism that we were naive in assuming that we could have CF-100's and other types in production back as early as 1950, when it takes such a long time to produce an original type from the drawing board. Because of that, or as the article expresses it because of the fanciful predictions at the political level, we have been lulled into lethargy, thinking that everything was well. I think the government should have taken the public, through the elected representatives of the people, into its confidence and explained the details, the problems and the circumstances. Had that been, done, I think we would have had greater co-operation from the public at large. It is a good thing that for the first time air force personnel intimately in touch with the problem are speaking out, in order to bring these difficulties to the attention of the public.
We do not criticize the F-86. It has proved its worth in operations in Korea. It is being sent as interim supplies to the R.A.F. until they can develop their own advanced types. The CF-100 likewise is going to serve a very useful purpose in the defence of Canada. My criticism is that the government has not been realistic in keeping the public and this house informed, rather choosing to lull us into a sense of well-being when there was no cause for such a feeling.

speechtext:
And nobody is overly enthusiastic on the other side. Continuing to deal with the problem of the defence of Canada, the No. 1 priority, according to the minister's white paper, is getting over the equipment difficulties so far as aircraft are concerned. I only hope-I have no information, because no information is forthcoming for hon. members-that in the production of aircraft we shall continue to keep abreast of the changing needs as we move toward the delta wing type of aircraft, or as it is presented in the Roundel for the current month, as we move toward "the turbo-jet, the ram-jet and the rocket air force of the future". Here is a very interesting article on that subject. That contains information that we could not possibly get in this house.
There is also the personnel problem. We discovered that in the lowering of the educational standards. The hon. member for Calgary East, in a reply he received, got the information that the educational standards for servicemen were constantly going down. I often wondered how the quality

of our personnel compares with that of other NATO troops, especially NATO airmen being trained in this country. I do not have the information on it but I would rather doubt, with the continuing lowering of standards, that we are finding it easy to maintain the necessary high levels to man the type of air force required by today's defence needs.
I notice that we are still emphasizing the sort of easy approach to defence in advertisements in the press. Here is an advertisement that appeared in the Carberry Express on January 28, 1953:
Security-Pension Responsible Position for
Young men
If you are over 17 years of age ... in good health. . . . eager for adventure, travel and fellowship in a large organization that offers real careers for young Canadians today . . . fill in the coupon below and get the full information about careers open to you in the Canadian army. You will be amazed at the wonderful opportunities for trade training . . . the good wages . . . benefits of all kinds including long annual holidays. Find out without obligation.
Well, that is offering a good time in the army when I think we should be emphasizing more the obligation and the responsibility to serve in the defence of freedom. It reminds me of the situation that existed during the 1930's when I was a young student. In 1936 we subscribed to that famous Oxford resolution that under no circumstances would we take up arms for king and for country, and three years later most of us who had subscribed to that view were involved in the bloodiest war that this world has ever seen. We seem to be still bogged down by the fallacy of nineteenth century Liberalism that believed we were moving gradually towards perfection and that if we only waited long enough everything would work out happily in the end, or, as the Fabians called it, the inevitability of gradualness. I believe that we should be emphasizing more the responsibility of service and the obligation to serve rather than feather-bedding the situation, as seems to be indicated by that advertisement.
Now, there is the reserve and the auxiliary problem. The reserve seems to be frustrated and the auxiliary seems to be frustrated, judging from the statements I have already indicated. From personal experience I know that we have not been able to make very good use of the auxiliary other than those who are actively engaged in the nine auxiliary squadrons, and even those do not seem to be too happy, judging from Rohmer and Northcott's remarks; but in the air force association frustration prevails because up to
Supply-National Defence the present time-and I am a member of of the association-the only part we have been able to take is in the form of a social club, to try to preserve the old camaraderie of world war II, to do a little line shooting in an atmosphere that is very similar to the wartime mess atmosphere.
We tried to assist recruiting, but there were not enough recruits offering themselves to require any assistance. We tried for the air observer corps, but we discovered no observer corps was being formed in our area so we participated in the mobilization air training plan; at least two of us did. I am glad to see this plan being expanded, because I think it is a very useful way to absorb those keen types who in the face of the present emergency and crisis want to do something more than reminisce about world war II.
Speaking personally, I have been trying to retain my interest in radar, because I think it is the most important avenue of service as we move toward the new type of air defence required in Canada; but under the M.A.T.P. I am earmarked as a personnel officer, a trade in which I have had absolutely no experience in the air force. All my experience was with night fighter airborne radar. We spent months and months in tedious training in aerial interception (A.I.) tactics, and now there seems to be no use for that particular activity. I find this very hard to understand in a day when the defence of Canada depends upon a supply of personnel skilled in the practices of
G.C.I. (ground controlled interception).
One final word on this problem of the defence of Canada. Judging by the statement in the white paper we are going to replace the present Vampires and Mustangs of reserve squadrons with the CF-100. That seems to be another one of these facile statements and so far as I am concerned it requires more elaboration. With the present type of training going on in the reserve squadrons, I am very sceptical whether it will be possible to bring the reserve crews up to the standards of efficiency required for radar-equipped CF-100 all-weather fighters and necessary to cope with any possible airborne attack. I remember my own long-extended training: a year in Canada, two months at an advanced flying unit to convert from singles to twins, four months on operational training and then on to blind approach training and further squadron training before becoming operational. From the time we graduated with wings until we became operational another year was absorbed in training. After we were trained we converted twice to new types of radar equipment, and we were taken out of the line of operations during the period
3898	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence of conversion. But this statement says-and apparently the reserve is still going to be the backbone, the main responsibility for Canadian defence-that the CF-100 will be supplied to the reserve and everything will work out for the best. All-weather flying of jet aircraft with airborne radar requires the most highly skilled type of crew. It is one of the most highly skilled types of activity in the air force. It means that we shall have to take into consideration real problems of reserve training in order to handle this responsibility.

Mr. Chairman, before the house rose at one o'clock the hon. member for Brandon had been speaking for some fifty minutes or so, and at one point in his speech he referred to an editorial in Canadian Aviation of April, 1952. At the time he gave the quotation I asked the hon. member if he thought that what he had selected from the editorial was fair, without reading the whole editorial as it appeared, simply using that quotation to try to support the kind of case he was making.
The fact is that this editorial was written at a time when a number of public statements had been made which were I think intended to make exactly the kind of case the hon. member was trying to make in his speech this morning. This editorial was written, not in support of that case but as an answer to the criticisms that were being made. It was for that reason that I questioned the hon. member on the careful selection he had made of one small part of the editorial. I think in fairness to everybody I should read the editorial as it appeared. This reads:
Facts Versus Rumours-An Appraisal of the Avro Projects
The rumour factory seems to be in quantity production on the subject of Avro Canada and more particularly the two high-priced projects, the CF-100 patrol interceptor and the Orenda jet engine. If we are to credit the anonymous but "well-informed" sources responsible for current reports, the CF-100 is a flying flop and the Orenda is crawling with technical "bugs". To sum it up, millions of tax dollars have been poured into Avro but only delays and alibis have come out of the factory.
What are the facts? It is true that since 1946 the government has consigned some $50 million to the Avro programs. It is also a fact that in terms of aircraft and engines produced to date, the return


on this substantial investment has been insignia fieant. On the other hand, what reason did we have to expect these projects to move from drafting board to quantity production in less than five years? Here are two reasons: 1. As a nation we have had no previous experience in appraising topflight aeronautical assignments of this kind.
This is the portion selected by the hon. member for his quotation:
2. The fanciful predictions at the political level have supported the naive assumption that such a process should be quick and simple.
Is the CF-100 fighter program shamefully sluggish? Here is the chronicle: Design project launched in October, 1946. Detailed design started in May,
1947.	Prototype tooling commenced in January,
1948.	Government contract for 10 pre-production fighters issued in May, 1949. First prototype CF-100 flown in January, 1950. Total elapsed time, design start to test flight: 40 months. Comparable British fighter prototypes have required 38 and 39 months to initial flight. A U.S. fighter got airborne in 34 months.
The original assignment was to build 10 CF-100 fighters. It was not until September, 1950, that a production order was issued and this was stepped up substantially in February of last year.
The record also reveals that time consumption on the Orenda development has not been out of line. The period from design to first test run: 29 months. U.S. average: 25 months. Two comparable British jets: 29 months average.
In February this year, the Orenda Mk. 2 (production version) completed, with success, its 150-hour type acceptance test run. This was 36 months after the initial run. U.S. average for this stage: 46 months. Comparable British average: 37 months.
In attempting to assess Avro's progress, it is only fair to note that conversion from experimental development to quantity production is quite an ordeal for any organization. In this instance it involved a drastic shake-up that split Avro down the middle to create engine and fighter divisions. The Orenda assignment has called for erection, in less than a year, of a new 400,000 square-foot plant. While the pilot production line in the original building continues to dribble out engines, the impressive ranks of machine tools are forming in the new plant and it is predicted that production will be flowing steadily before the end of this year. Meantime, fighter production has been retarded for spar modification and for important armament changes. Such delays are a familiar feature of military aircraft progress. On the strength of factual evidence we believe it is fair to concede that these two projects are proceeding without significant delay.
The editorial then goes on to discuss briefly the quality of the aircraft and of the engine which I do not think is relevant to the argument the hon. member was making. The editorial concludes as follows:
The CF-100 is neither substandard nor obsolete. It was recognized after flight testing of the prototype that the main spar would have to be strengthened to prevent undue wing flexing under the high G stress of military aerobatics. The two prototype versions delivered to the R.C.A.F. and shortly returned to the manufacturer for modification had been placarded (with a 5 G limitation) pending this modification.
This aircraft was designed to meet a particular military specification combining exceptional range, all-weather night and day operation, high rate of climb, and effective speed for combat. There are

very few aircraft in the world today in this particular bracket. And until one of this type with superior performance comes along, the CF-100 can't be described with accuracy as obsolete. Critical examination of government investments such as the Avro projects is a right of the public and a responsibility of the press. But criticism is only helpful when it is sound. And rumours are poor substitutes for facts.
I am content, Mr. Chairman, to leave my question to the hon. member, who has made a quotation from that editorial in support of the argument he has been making, and the reading of the editorial to speak for themselves. Perhaps I might also say in addition that the final sentence of the editorial can, I think, with great justice and with advantage be applied to a very great majority of the criticisms that we have been hearing not only in this debate but also over the past two or three years from the official opposition regarding defence matters, namely, that rumours are poor substitutes for facts.
