I think it brings out the point I was trying to make even more clearly than hitherto. As the hon. member will recall, the point I made at the beginning of my remarks last evening was that information has not been forthcoming concerning some of the major defence developments, particularly with reference to air. As a result of the rumour-mongering that has arisen from lack of information, there has been much unnecessary criticism of these very excellent projects. I agree entirely that A. V. Roe and Canadair have done an excellent job, but it is unfortunate that members of the house could not have been taken into the confidence of the Department of National Defence so that unnecessary rumours might have been allayed.
I also made the point at the opening of my remarks that we in the opposition have to go to magazine and newspaper reports in order to get the facts, and that is an unfortunate state of affairs. The editorial that has just been read indicates that situation precisely. I was not fully aware of developments on the CF-100 project and the Orenda engine until I received all the necessary information from various Canadian aviation magazines. We in the house are treated to broad optimistic generalities rather than the specific information that is necessary in order to discuss the very important problems of defence development intelligently and in a meaningful way.
Supply-National Defence
The phrase "not in the public interest" is used repeatedly when we are looking for information on these problems. The hon. member for Nanaimo asked for information on radar development which he was denied. We had to get the information from a publication of the air force association. I would venture to say that espionage agents know more about the defence program than we in the opposition. I think we would have a happier state of affairs so far as defence matters are concerned if the government were willing to take members on all sides of the house into their confidence and treat them as reasonable beings having a sense of responsibility in these matters and as official representatives of the citizens of Canada, because in the final analysis, no matter how we try to conceal the true facts of the real situation, the burden is going to fall upon the shoulders of the public. They are the ones who inevitably have to bear the brunt. Therefore I thank the hon. member for Halifax for putting the editorial on the record because it very precisely and effectively climaxes the important point that I was trying to make in my remarks.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I was rather surprised by the attitude of the hon. member who has just spoken and who is one of our most likeable colleagues. He forgets one thing, that no minister of national defence has afforded as many opportunities to members of parliament to visit plants where jet planes are made and other plants that supply arms and ammunition as the present Minister of National Defence. I wonder if the hon. gentleman was a member of parliament when we went to Toronto a couple of years ago and visited the A. V. Roe plant at Malton. Nothing was hidden from us. There were gentlemen there who were willing to show and explain everything to all members of parliament who were there, and they were not only Liberal members. There were many Conservatives and members belonging to other groups. We were together and that visit was very interesting and most informative.
Now, sir, you may find me a little old-fashioned but I do not understand the propriety of discussing technical matters concerning arms and ammunition in the house. There are some things that are supposed to be secret but nothing should be secret to a member of parliament. He has the right to be informed, but I wonder if it would not be a good thing to discuss all these matters in camera. Some gentlemen of the press might complain about it because they would not have the opportunity to hear the discussion that took place in the house, but members of
3900	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence parliament would have the opportunity to become much better acquainted with all these matters without any publicity. I presume that the hon. gentleman who has just spoken was not at all seeking publicity and that he was fulfilling his parliamentary duties in speaking as he did. I am sure that was his purpose.
But on the other hand if we look at the newspapers we see that they give very detailed and precise information about matters that should remain secret, and I maintain the view that discussions like this one should be held in camera notwithstanding the complaints that may come from the press. When members of parliament are properly informed about any matter, they cannot ask for anything more unless they want to play politics.
I stand by the minister and I also stand by my own attitude in the house with regard to military matters and with regard to two incidents that occurred in Quebec city. Something very serious happened during the Quebec conference. We all remember, as it appeared in the press, that the plans for the invasion of Normandy were lost in the reading room of the Chateau Frontenac. They were top secret documents; and they were left there by an officer who was absent-minded -whether American, English or Canadian I do not know. But that top secret document, the most secret document of the time, was left there by someone who was perhaps absent-minded, perhaps drunk, perhaps crazy- probably all three. But, now, what did we see in the press afterwards? We saw that a sergeant had been rewarded, had been given a decoration because he had found those papers-and quite properly so. But we did not see in any paper, and I have not been told by anyone, that the officer guilty of that gross negligence has been punished. One was rewarded; the other was not punished.
The result was this. It occurred again, and it was reported in all the papers and particularly in the Ottawa Journal of November 7 of last year:
Reporters Hear 'Top Secret'-on Upper Shelf
Quebec City, Nov. 7-(BUP)-Two reporters rode down in a Chateau Frontenac elevator with 15 civilians and senior officers attending the Canadian-British-U.S. military conference.
One officer turned to the other and asked: "Can I borrow those documents you have?"
Answer: "I'm sorry, I can't do it-top secret you know. But you'll find them in my room . . . on the upper shelf in the clothes closet".

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Did they fire the manager of the hotel too?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
No, they did not fire the manager of the hotel at all. But, because


there was no sanction of the first offence a second one occurred which was reported by the press.
Do you not find it serious, Mr. Chairman? I cannot conceive that men who are supposed to keep the old army tradition and make the necessary distinction between what is important and what is not could come to be guilty of such an offence. I am not telling you, sir, anything that is unknown. I only remind you of what you know and, I hope, the consequences too.
May I tell you, sir, that I am much more interested in Korea than in Currie; and we have heard so much about Currie that I hope that I may be excused if I talk about Korea. I have great respect for the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) and I believe that he has done a quite superhuman job, especially before the appointment of his associate minister. That does not mean that I have always agreed with him and that I take for granted everything that is said by the Department of National Defence; but I believe sincerely that he has done a good job under the circumstances and that none of his critics could have done better under similar circumstances. Now, sir, what astounds me is that external affairs and the army are intermingled to such a point that it is impossible to discuss army matters without discussing external policy, and vice versa. Very often the Minister of National Defence had to speak about external matters, matters of external policy, and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) had to speak about military matters. I will speak about both.
Mr. Chairman, I remember that about three years ago, when it was decided that Canada should take part in the police force that was to settle the Korean problem, everyone was under the impression that the destroyer that was sent by Canada to Korea would arrive in Korea when everything was over. One remembers also, Mr. Chairman, that President Roosevelt some years ago, immediately after the war with Japan, decided to "liberate" Korea. That was the expression used by the then president. He wanted to free the Koreans from all Japanese influence. It was a noble aim, but afterwards it was decided that Korea would be divided in two by the 38th parallel; and that there would be a police force in the south-an American police force. What happened was that the American officers who were there were under no control, and one of the top ranking officers was m love with a mistress of the chief of the communists of North Korea. That woman succeeded in helping the smuggling

of arms from South Korea to North Korea and that is the reason why North Korea became at one time well equipped in arms and ammunition. That has been published in Coronet, a United States magazine.
Well, there were battles in Korea but there was no declaration of war-so much so that sometime ago a young American soldier who carried double risk insurance was killed in Korea and, according to the press, his family after consulting eminent lawyers decided to take legal action against the insurance company, under the claim that there was no war in Korea, that it was only a police action, and that the insurance which did not cover war risks was in force for that man who was fighting as a policeman in Korea. The United States tribunal which studied the case in the first instance gave judgment in favour of the family, and that judgment was appealed by the insurance company. The appeal court confirmed the judgment of the first instance, showing that it was a police action that was being undertaken in Korea. Approximately three years ago when it was decided to send a Canadian destroyer to Korea, I warned the Secretary of State for External Affairs that that was a very dangerous step, to be tco much under the influence of the foreign policy of the United States. It was abused by some of the newspapers, in these times of human rights and fundamental freedoms, because I had taken advantage of my human rights and fundamental freedoms.
Since then, many important statements have been made. I recall reading in Le Soleil of Quebec, February 14 last year, a very well written and timely article under the pen of one of the most brilliant journalists in Canada, the former president of the press gallery, Mr. Lorenzo Pare. He said that it was then time to get out of Korea. One may say that it is the prerogative of military men to express views on military matters, and that it is their exclusive right to make pronunciamentos in that regard. Well, some important gentlemen have spoken to that effect. General Mark Clark, for instance, is quoted by the Ottawa Journal of September 26, 1952, in an editorial entitled "This Bleak Prospect in Korea". He said:
The sober reality today in Korea is that there is no fresh and concrete evidence to indicate any increase in the reds' desire for a truce.
Then the Journal continues:
General Clark's grave words come with the Panmunjom 'truce' talks virtually suspended, and while hot water in Korea grows hotter.
Supply-National Defence
The same editorial, dating back eight months ago, quotes Major General Selden, who had just returned from Korea. He said:
Twice as many United Nations troops and half again as much air power would insure a decisive allied victory in Korea.
After having made these two quotations, the Journal concludes:
It may be, as so many argue, that we can't risk all-out war with China: that we can't do much more than we are doing in Korea lest it bring such war with China. But against that, can we risk or afford a continuation of what is happening in Korea now, with its bleak prospect of years of costly indecision, and with exposure to the Russians of both weakness and fear?
On September 25 last year, Mr. Clement Davies, Liberal party leader in the British House of Commons, suggested a quick plan for disarmament, to be supervised by a United Nations police force. On Thursday, October 2, 1952, Major General A. J. H. Cassels had a hunch that there would be a Korean armistice within six or nine months from that date. Therefore the pourparler that is taking place now was foreseen by officers of high standing.
There was something else that occurred last year, and that was the Truman-Eisen-hower controversy about the campaign in Asia, and what former President Truman said was reported in the newspapers of October 1. Two days later the newspapers carried General Eisenhower's answer, and I need only read the headline:
Ike tells isolationist area U.S. should not have fought.
General suggests America should not have gone to war against Kaiser, Hitler; leave Asia to Asians.
Well, this statement is most important, because it came from the lips of the general who commanded the allied forces during the last war. What I find very refreshing is the change of administration in the Pentagon at Washington. Just because the United States is a friendly neighbour, one should not be precluded from expressing an honest opinion about matters of such tremendous importance which mean life or death for countless people. When I think of that beautiful country, full of tradition, that rich country that was Korea, and when we see the mountains of ruins in all the cities of that formerly prosperous country, I wonder how that country has been liberated, to use the words of President Roosevelt.
Well, sir, I have many quotations that I could use, but I shall abstain from doing so because I do not want to make a long speech at this stage of the session. But my conclusion, sir, is this. The Minister of National Defence and also the Secretary of State for External Affairs, to whom I give certain credit
3902	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence for his efforts for peace, should see to it that even within the United Nations Canada should express an independent opinion-one that is not biased by that of the United States or of Great Britain-until a common decision is made. We are partners. It happens that under NATO the forces should be under one command and should have one policy. But it is important that those who attend such conferences should not be impressed by the other delegates who represent larger countries. They must express the sentiments and the feelings of the Canadian people before giving a power of attorney to the other delegates who speak in their behalf. Therein lies the superiority of NATO over the United Nations.
In the United Nations everything was run by the security council; everything was run by the great nations, and the other countries like Canada were not on a footing of equality with the big ones. In the next conference I hope that the Minister of National Defence and also the Secretary of State for External Affairs for Canada will continue to impress upon their fellow delegates the importance of Canada as a great nation. If the population of Canada is not as large as that of the United States, Great Britain, Russia, France, or the other countries of Europe or of China, nevertheless it is a great country in the noblest meaning of that word. By that I mean that Canada has reached the point where she should be considered by all to be on a footing of equality in the international discussions in which our ministers and delegates take part.
In conclusion may I say that I hope the efforts made by the government-I do not say by the ministers alone but rather by the government-to promote peace in the world at the earliest possible opportunity will have the full support of all those who belong to NATO and also of those who belong to the United Nations.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in rising to speak in this debate I fully admit my limited capacity to speak with authority on this subject. What I have to say will be based on listening to debates in the House of Commons and on my experience on the defence expenditure committee. I will also convey to the minister some of the things that have been expressed to me by a good number of my constituents.
With the knowledge that some 45 per cent of the taxes collected today are being spent on defence, I am quite sure that all members of the committee realize the necessity for making as certain as possible that there are no unnecessary expenditures in this extremely large-spending department. I never rise to speak on this question without thinking of the workers in the smelters, the mines, the forests, the factories, the offices and on the


farms of Canada whose hard labour, and the taxes which result from that hard labour, make it possible to carry on and to continue this defence program. I am sure they are willing to pay what is necessary to provide adequate defence for this country; but I am sure they would be most unwilling to pay what was unnecessary.
We must realize at this time that all those people who are contributing considerable taxes from their modest incomes are doing without many things they would otherwise enjoy were it not necessary to provide for these defence estimates. May I also say, Mr. Chairman, that I think we are making an exceptional defence effort. I think it is quite correct to say that for purposes of defence we are paying a greater percentage of the taxes collected than is any western European country. I understand that the average there is somewhere about 32 per cent.
Whenever I am listening to debates on defence or am starting to speak on defence, I am always reminded of a statement made by the hon. member for Nanaimo and to be found in Hansard of May 10, 1951, at page 2810. I never forgot that statement because when the hon. member made it he spoke with a lifetime of experience and with knowledge. I accept that statement as founded in fact. The hon. gentleman said:
I have never known an admiral, a general or an air marshal who did not begin by asking for more than his share of anything.
I have always kept that statement in my mind when I have been dealing with defence matters because I think it puts into good language what happens in military circles not only in Canada but in other countries. It indicates a more or less inevitable development of the military mind.
The scandal at Camp Petawawa was revealed as the result of the action of a responsible and patriotic citizen in sending an anonymous letter to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. It was not discovered by the defence department. It was discovered by the alertness of one citizen. I hope that all citizens of Canada continue to be just as alert as was that gentleman.
That scandal was discovered and as a result of the discovery of it the minister ordered Mr. George Currie to conduct an investigation into the whole situation in the army works services. This investigation proved without question that at Petawawa-and it was an exceptional case, we admit-as a result of a conspiracy, a gang of crooks had organized to loot and to steal public property. In addition to that, there is no doubt that the Currie report revealed an unfortunate state of affairs throughout a considerable section of the army works services.

As a result of that investigation and as a result of debates in the House of Commons- and they should never be underestimated, although we all at times get tired of listening to repetitious remarks-there is no doubt about it that there is a great improvement across Canada at this time. I have heard that from my constituents; I have heard it also from friends in the services. There is an improvement in the administration of the Department of National Defence. In fact, I am told that the pendulum has swung a bit too far the other way and that now if you want to paint a screen door you must get authority from Ottawa. That is typical of the defence department, and the military mind. It naturally goes from one extreme to another. But I am told that is a fact. In any event, I think we are all extremely pleased to know that there is a considerable improvement.
I might say at this point that to me there is an interesting aspect of these debates as far as my correspondence is concerned. I have had to explain repeatedly to some of my constituents that the so-called Murray report dealt with the United States forces and not the Canadian forces.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: No, no.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
Constituents have written and told me about the dreadful waste on the Alaska highway, and that sort of thing. I have had to write back and tell them it had nothing to do with Canada, that it was waste by United States forces there during the second world war.
As a member of the defence expenditure committee, I have had an opportunity to hear witnesses from the Department of Defence Production. I must say in fairness that I have formed the opinion that they are an honest, competent group of officials who have been working under particularly difficult conditions. Without doubt, though, Mr. Chairman, the evidence clearly indicates that in the defence construction program there has been waste and extravagance. But I do not blame the officials of Defence Construction Limited. I am trying to be fair in this whole question. Their handicaps have been the results of a set of unusual circumstances. The first was the inevitable sense of haste and urgency. In fairness I think we must admit that we do not do things as well under abnormal conditions as under normal conditions when we can take the normal time to plan a project, develop it and so forth.
Second, there were shortages of material, particularly of steel, which caused delays, and which in turn caused increased expenses and excessive costs, and so on. That was not their fault.
Supply-National Defence
The third important thing was that, after listening to the evidence, I came to the conclusion that there were delays and increased expenses occasioned first of all by the program as designed by the armed forces. They say what they want, and it is obvious to me in many cases they started out on a project without knowing exactly what they did want, and then after they got started in some instances major changes were made in design. These things caused increased expenses, and no doubt in some cases there was no justification for it. On top of all that we had this program going on under difficult weather conditions, with the construction industry naturally looking for its profits as usual. I think that that combination of circumstances did produce conditions which meant extra cost, some extravagance and some waste, but I certainly would not lay the blame on the honest and competent officials of Defence Construction Limited. After listening to their evidence in the committee I think it is fair to say that one cannot fail to be impressed by the magnitude of the task, the unusual problems they had to meet, the urgency of the program and these other factors that I have mentioned.
Defence Construction is commissioned to build what the armed forces consider they require. I am of the opinion there is every evidence, as Mr. Currie said in his report on the army works services, of a tendency toward war psychology among certain of the high officials of the defence department. Many of these men obtained their experience in the second world war, and public money is nothing to them when trying to get things done. They were impressed, and rightly so, by the urgency of the situation and the element of speed, and they allowed themselves to be carried away. Money apparently was no object whatever when things had to be done. That has had a big effect on the cost of the program today. Buildings were frequently delayed, as I said before, because of change in designs and plans. I am distinctly under the impression, because of that war psychology that Mr. Currie mentioned, that the senior officials in the armed forces gave little thought to costs when planning the building programs and bringing them to fruition. These people look on things from an entirely different point of view when compared with the average Canadian citizen. They have lived a different life; in fact I have said to some of them, and I know some of them who are bitterly opposed to socialism, that they live the life of the most complete social security of any people of Canada. They are cared for from the cradle to the grave, and naturally they have not

Supply-National Defence the same approach as the man in the street who is struggling along making a living, and being taxed to pay for these things. That was indicated when the program was first started by the purchase of new desks and furniture.
I am told, and I should like the minister to correct me if I am wrong, that quite serviceable desks were taken out and, I understand, taken down to public works and brand new desks of a finer type were brought in. Expensive rugs were bought. I am quite sure that these new desks and these expensive carpets did very little to increase the defence effort or contribute to the greater defence of Canada. In that connection, Mr. Chairman, I want to read briefly from an article in the Globe and Mail of November 20, 1952, by George Bain:
Two years' purchases Defence rugs, carpets cost $839,903
In less than two years. $839,903 worth of rugs and carpets have been ordered by the Department of National Defence.
At $17 a square yard-more than most Canadian householders pay for floor-covering-this would buy enough broadloom to cover Yonge street, curb-to-curb from King street almost to Roxborough street.
On this rug, all the 100,000 men and women of Canada's active navy, army and air force could be assembled-two to a yard-without crowding.
The total of the defence department's rug orders is derived from the lists of major defence contracts which have been published twice monthly since November 20, 1950.
This is how the rug-buying breaks down by years:
Between November 20 and the end of 1950, contracts were placed for $54,865 worth of rugs.
In 1951, five orders added $141,403 to the total.
And up to the end of October this year-the last date covered by the contracts lists-$643,635 worth had been ordered.
In the same 23 months since November, 1950, contracts in a total of $452,929 were made for linoleum. All but one of these was awarded in 1951, when linoleum purchases amounted to $428,929.
Retail prices quoted here for top quality linoleum are $4 a square yard for blue, $3.45 a square yard for brown-the colours in which it is presumed the defence purchasers would be most interested.
At an average price of $3.75 a yard, $452,929 would buy more than 114,000 square yards of linoleum. Even with allowance made for the cost of installation, which would reduce the yardage, the amount purchased still could be reckoned in acres -about 24 of them.
To go with the new rugs and linoleum, the defence department in same period-a period in which the strength of the services increased by fewer than 55,000 men-ordered about $8,650,000 worth of furniture.
Some of this has been office furniture-filing cabinets, tables, office safes (79,671 this year) and the like-but the largest number of contracts listed have been simply for "furniture".
Defence headquarters and the country's navy, army and air force bases were not without furniture when the new, post-Korea defence program was embarked upon.

And so on. I think that very extensive ordering of rugs-and there are some very expensive rugs in some of the offices of defence headquarters; you fairly sink into them when you walk on them-and this expensive linoleum and these expenses for furniture show that these people were going to have their offices in good shape as soon as they had the money to carry on and do it with.
I am going to pass from there to bring to the attention of the minister something that several of my constituents have mentioned to me, men of experience in the Royal Navy and in the Royal Canadian Navy. I have no capacity to speak on the subject, but I am just passing on to the minister the criticisms that have come to me from men with senior naval experience. They are of the opinion that there is a danger for us in this country to get delusions of grandeur as far as the navy is concerned and consider going in for large ships. I should like the minister to tell the committee what is the daily cost of running the Magnificent and if the government is considering building another aircraft carrier of that type. What does it cost per day to run a cruiser?
I have a clipping here from the Montreal Gazette of December 18, 1951, which deals with the Canadian naval policy as laid out by Admiral Mainguy. This reads:
Mainguy Stresses Anti-Sub Defence Sees Major R.C.N. Role Under NATO in Combating Undersea Menace
Ottawa, Dec. 17-Major role of the R.C.N. under the North Atlantic Treaty Organization is antisubmarine warfare, Vice-Admiral E. R. Mainguy said today.
The admiral who this month took over command of the R.C.N. and who two years ago wrote the "Mainguy Report" on the navy's internal problems, said at a conference in the parliamentary press gallery that he, as chief of the naval staff, is "against" any R.C.N. activity or development which does not have to do with anti-submarine work or the defence of harbours.
The admiral said in a speech recently that there was no reason why Canada should not become the anti-sub authority of the allied powers.
At today's conference he said Canada's naval role had been discussed at NATO conferences, and it was generally considered that Canada's main responsibility is anti-submarine work.
When the minister replies I should like him to tell the committee what are the intentions of the government with respect to building large ships for the navy.
I have very little to say at this time with regard to the army except that a number of my constituents have said to me that it appears to be rather expensive advertising when it costs $161 to secure each recruit.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: The corrected figure is $70 per active force man or $43 if you include the reserves.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
I got the figure of $161 from another person and I am glad to be corrected. That is the figure that people have written me about and I will see that it is corrected.
I listened with a great deal of interest yesterday to the speech of the hon. member for Cape Breton South. I think he made a most excellent speech and dealt with some aspects of defence in a unique and somewhat unusual way.
He spoke at some length about the morale of the troops in Germany and Korea. I mention this also because a number of my constituents have written to me and I have met a number of men who have returned from Korea and Germany and there are complaints about the welfare services in those countries. The hon. member for Brandon spoke at some length on this matter earlier today. I have another clipping from the Montreal Gazette of December 8,	1952, dealing with this
question. This is entitled "Troop Morale in Germany Said 'Rotten' ". It sets out interviews with various men who have returned from overseas and who were complaining about the lack of recreational facilities and so on.
I am definitely in favour of the suggestion made by the hon. member for Brandon that civilian recreational services for the troops should be provided if possible. I know that they rendered great service during the first and second world wars. I want to make my plea that everything be done to make living conditions as good as possible for those men who are away from Canada. The minister may have some explanation of the present form of welfare services that are being provided, but I would like him to tell the committee just what is being done at the present time. I think there is a general complaint across the country, and I know I have received complaints from my constituents that the welfare services overseas are not all that they should be.
Dealing with the air force I must say that here I will have to depend upon what other people say. I was disturbed by an article which appeared in the Globe and Mail of March 27 entitled, "Time People Given Truth, Rohmer Says". The article continues:
Addressing a meeting of the Canadian Progress Club at the Royal York hotel, he continued: "Canada could not put up a single modern aircraft in its own defence. (She) is absolutely helpless to an air attack".
His main charges:
The air defence of Canada is entrusted to nine auxiliary fighter squadrons equipped with hopeless, obsolescent aircraft and manned by part-time pilots.

Apparently that article was reprinted in many Canadian papers and has caused great concern to many Canadians. I should like the minister to deal particularly with the charges made by this retired air force officer and tell the committee exactly what is the situation.
There is another aspect of defence in which I am particularly interested and in which a great number of people across the country are interested. Many people are of the opinion that in recent years there has been a tendency for parliament to lose control of these vast expenditures and for civilian control to be lessened and lessened. This has been a gradual development. In this respect I should like to quote briefly from Comment of June, 1951. This is an excellent magazine which deals with economic and social questions. I think it will save time to quote this article because it sets out succinctly what I have in mind. It reads:
Military Must Accept Civilian Control
The experience of recent months has graphically illustrated the importance of civilian control over military forces.
Military commanders must have a good deal of power and authority so that they can direct the forces at their disposal effectively. But military commanders derive their authority from appointment and not from democratic elections. They are not responsible to the people but must be held absolutely responsible to the civilian representatives of the people who appoint them.
And again:
The principle of civic control over the armed forces of the nation has long been accepted in the United Kingdom and in other nations which derive their constitutional practices from the traditions of the British parliamentary system. But the evolution of modern methods of defence, warfare and international security action may call for closer scrutiny of the way in which this principle is being applied.
We of this group agree with those sentiments. We believe that we should watch to make certain that there is proper civilian control of the military in connection with the expansion of our defence program. We feel that decisions are made by the military with regard to large expenditures that should be made by civilian authorities. They have had their way as to what was required here and there. We do urge that there be stricter control of the military and greater reference to parliament with regard to these large expenditures. In many cases all that parliament does is to confirm the total amounts when knowing little about the

Supply-National Defence details until after the money has been expended. Apparently Mr. Currie was of the same opinion because he makes this suggestion in his report:
Alternative No. 2
The second alternative is to create a civilian organization running parallel to a military organization up through commands to army headquarters. This alternative would-
1. Relieve military personnel of most of the administrative function and enable them to concentrate on planning and on executive direction of works.
2.	Open up career possibilities to civilians and thus attract high calibre permanent personnel and provide stability to administration now difficult to achieve.
The advantage of this course of action would appear to be the combining of greater administrative stability and efficiency with a valuable training element for R.C.K. personnel.
He had in mind there a more or less parallel civilian organization. As I understand it, at the present time huge quantities of valuable buildings and supplies are handed over to the armed forces and they are not made directly responsible for accounting for them. So far as the quartermaster general's branch is concerned, there should be a civilian check and audit on the whole quartermaster general's department so that they will be responsible for equipment and supplies to a civilian authority, with that civilian authority responsible to the minister's officials. As I said before, in our opinion parliament under present conditions has very little to say about the major decisions involving large expenditures. The military people decide what they want regardless of cost and go ahead and spend the money. In our opinion a system must be devised whereby there will be more civilian control of the defence program through the parliament of this country.
I want to deal now with a different aspect of the question. I understand that the present defence program was designed with a view to a peak in our expenditures being reached in 1954-55, but present events should cause some consideration to be given to a levelling off of that program. There is not the sense of urgency; we can continue to carry out the program over a longer period of years, and on that account there should be some opportunity in the near future for reducing our expenditures on the military aspects of national defence. With the defence construction program nearly completed, it should be possible to save considerable sums of money in that quarter.
A few months ago a United States commission conducted an investigation into the armed forces of that country, and it was their honest opinion that a 10 per cent reduction in defence expenditures could be achieved
[Mr. Herridge.l
through the elimination of waste occasioned by haste and speed without affecting the adequate defence of the country. That period is passing in the United States as it is here, and there is more control by congress over defence expenditures and so on. Even this year in my opinion the minister could save $200 million by insisting on economy and doing away with frills and so on, which saving could be used by way of economic aid as a part of our defence program and thus give some positive evidence to the world of our desire to go at least half way in the effort toward world peace.
There has been certain optimism in recent weeks because of the apparently changed position of the Soviet leaders. Past experience would cause us to proceed with caution, but I do think it is quite safe to say, just as the hon. member for Temiscouata said, that the Canadian people want the government to speak up for Canada and say in a very positive way that we are willing to do all that is fair and possible to promote world peace and to go at least half-way in that direction.
In going over some figures recently, I noticed that the subsidy to A. V. Roe Limited for the development of the jet airliner was $6,648,363.50, and that total subsidies to A. V. Roe Limited were over $63 million, mostly for the Orenda engine and CF-lOO's. I am not going into the question of whether or not that was a warranted expenditure. I am not competent to say but I do want to say that $63 million is ten times as much as we are spending on technical aid today. If we could reduce our defence expenditures by $200 million in the year or two ahead, what possibilities that would offer for the Canadian people to make a big contribution in the form of economic aid; first, economic aid under the North Atlantic treaty; second, rehabilitation of Korea; and, third, through technical assistance to substandard countries.
More than that, not only would we be making a gesture that would be a challenge to other countries of the world but we would also be doing something very sound and concrete to stabilize our agriculture. I am sure that the Minister of Agriculture would like to have a few of the millions that are being spent on defence to spend on floor price support for certain agricultural commodities. I am certain that the Canadian people would welcome the opportunity to make a magnificent gesture by contributing from $200 million to $400 million for economic aid, the rehabilitation of Korea and technical assistance to substandard countries. In doing so, we would not only be helping others but would be stabilizing the agricultural economy

of Canada and taking positive action in the development of world peace.

It makes it again very obvious, Mr. Chairman, that if we are ever going to have any kind of efficiency check-up and clean-up of the waste and extravagance that becomes more obvious every day in the operations of this government, it can only be done by bringing in somebody from outside, like Mr. Currie, who has proper qualifications and can look at the picture with an unbiased eye.
To do that would be simply following the principles that have long been established in the business world. After all, we have got to remember that this defence department is the biggest business in the country, doing about $2 billion worth of business every year; and a great many operations in the defence department are exactly similar to operations within any big, successful, commercial corporation.
In the business world it is well known that you cannot expect a departmental manager to report upon himself because, if he does, he is simply showing up the things that he should have done and the things that he should not have done. Periodically in large and successful business operations efficiency experts from outside are called in. They are not magicians but only people who have studied the most

satisfactory operations in the most successfully run commercial businesses. They take a look at the business they are investigating and, having no pet theories, no pet personnel, no ghosts in the closet to cover up, they say what that business operation is doing wrong. They make an unbiased report and, if that report is acted upon, as it is in business, the savings are usually far beyond the wildest dreams of the people running the company.
From practical experience I can say that it is impossible to know where you are being inefficient when you are close to the business, as you are when you are operating within a corporation. It is the kind of thing that we have urged this government to do with the various departments, particularly the Department of National Defence, but it seems that this government just does not want to listen to that kind of thing. I admit that, but surely the same is true of Great Britain and the United States. It has been suggested also by the defence department that the lack of conscription in Canada is a contributing factor. I think that, to a degree, that explanation is reasonable, but I do not think it can explain such a huge disparity.
The government says there is no waste or extravagance in defence spending. Well, I suggest that these per capita costs indicate that there is either waste or extravagance or gross mismanagement. I challenge the Minister of National Defence or one of his parliamentary assistants to tell the Canadian people why our figures are so out of line if there is no waste or extravagance.

There is only one other aspect of our defence program which concerns me as a layman and which I should like to mention at this time. I seriously question the wisdom of this nation pioneering, as it has been doing, in the field of advanced military weapons. It seems to me that this phase of defence could be better undertaken by our allies, Great Britain and the United States, who have greater facilities. For example, in recent years Canada has spent hundreds of millions of dollars, as has been pointed out today, experimenting in the field of advanced military aviation. Much of that work has been duplicated by other NATO countries.
Let us take the CF-100 project which has been bandied about a good deal today. I think it is obvious that for about four years this project has been dawdling along very slowly. The latest figures I have seen show that it has cost the taxpayer roughly $130 million, and about 16 planes have come off the assembly line. I think it is obvious to an unbiased observer that this CF-100 project, if it is not a fiasco, is at least a very costly experiment. I recall that the F-86 project was started at roughly the same time under United States licence. My understanding is that about 700 F-86 planes have come off the assembly line. I think there is a lesson to be learned from that comparison. It may give us a sense of real pride to read of Canada's achievements in this field, but I think at the same time parliament should keep in mind the staggering costs to the taxpayer. In addition, there is always the danger of one of these advanced weapons bogging down some place between the blueprint stage and the production stage.
We have read newspaper reports to the effect that the department is planning on going into further advanced fields in so far as military planes are concerned. I have seen the figure of $100 million bandied about for a new fighter. I think such costs are

unnecessary, and I contend that the taxpayers could save millions of dollars and still we could have weapons which were just as effective or better if, instead of taking on the present headaches of pioneering and design, we were to leave those to Britain and the United States. Then we could manufacture under licence in this country the best weapons which those countries could produce. It would be much less costly, and I think we would have just as good or better weapons.
I hope that before this debate is concluded the minister will tell me if there is something wrong with that suggestion. I have other suggestions to make during this discussion, but I shall leave them until the details of the estimates are being considered.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a word or two on the first item in the estimates of the Department of National Defence. Like the speaker who has preceded me, I do not claim to be an expert on defence. As a matter of fact I have never fired an army gun in my life. I have never been in the army, the navy or the air force, and know very little about that. The last gun I ever fired was a 12-gauge shotgun, and it kicked so badly it knocked me over and I lost my hat. However, I got the bird.
While I do not claim to be an expert, nevertheless I am interested in the defence of our country. I have personal reasons also for being interested. I had three sons, one of whom I lost in the war. Of the other two Who went through the last war, one is at present a flight lieutenant in the Canadian air force.
I wish to speak on what I might term broad policies with respect to defence. I have always adopted the view that it is best to be strong for the purposes of self-preservation. I have not been a keen critic of the defence department. I have more or less left such responsibility with the government as a responsibility of trust. I have never criticized individual expenditures unless such expenditures may have affected my own constituents in some direct fashion.
If I have been critical at all, it has always been of broad policies such as those which existed during the war; I refer, for instance, to the policy of the conscription of men, whether necessary or unnecessary, and to broad questions affecting war measures which involve defence policy at large. After all, I feel that policy with respect to war, defence and international relations governing defence are the more important issues. Therefore as I rise to speak on this item I feel impelled to say a word or two with respect to policy.
