Toward the conclusion of his speech yesterday, when the estimates of his department were introduced, the minister welcomed the apparent shift in Soviet policy. I am sure we all welcome any change in policy that will lead to a better understanding between the nations of the world and particularly between the Soviet and what we generally term the western or free democratic nations of the world. The policy now apparently adopted by the Soviets looks to be one designed to thaw out the cold-war policy that has existed in the world for a number of years.
Even though the minister may have welcomed this shift in Soviet policy, it seems to me that one or two questions must be asked and that those questions should be answered. The one question that gives me a good deal of concern-and it must give the minister similar concern-is whether or not communism itself ever changes, or whether communism always remains the ruthless ambition for world dominance and world dictatorship. If the answer to that question is that communism never changes, even though communist tactics may, then we must conclude that the present shift in policy is a tactical one. If we come to that conclusion, then we must ask ourselves the question:	What is the reason for this
tactical shift in Soviet policy?
If I am not mistaken, the general consensus is that the Soviet have always played their cards with some expectancy that what they call the capitalist system would eventually collapse; and by carrying on a cold-war policy which to some extent has avoided a universal war, they have hoped that the economies of the western democratic world would collapse. If such an event took place, then of course they expected that the result would be a depression of such great proportions that the western democratic world would be a fertile breeding ground for communism, and that it would become strong within the democratic countries.
I think it is conceded by some that one thing that is keeping the economies of the western nations-and I should say particularly the North American economies-in a reasonably prosperous position is the vast amounts of money being appropriated for defence, a fact which is reflected in a fairly high level of industrial activity and employment. I think it is generally believed that should reasonable assurance of peace be accepted, thus bringing about a condition where defence preparations would not be so necessary, we would consequently be headed for a business recession and perhaps a very serious economic depression.
The question that should be asked is what policies v/ould be pursued. The government of the day should be farsighted enough to be
3912	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence able to answer the question as to what policies, financial or otherwise, they are now contemplating to prevent the occurrence of a business recession or a depression. This is a question that has been asked on previous occasions, if not directly at least by very direct inference over and over again. Yet to my knowledge the government has never sufficiently answered the question. It is a very important one because the people who have to pay the bills ought to know. If Soviet calculations are correct that what they call a capitalist collapse is within the realm of possibility, then what policies would the government pursue? We have yet to have that question answered, and it is an important one.
There is another question that should be answered; and I am aware of the fact that in concluding his speech yesterday the minister was very careful to state the reason he was asking for such vast sums of money. I have gone over the last page of his speech very carefully. The minister is an able gentleman. He was not speaking from a prepared manuscript, but I daresay he watched every tiny word and every tiny comma in the conclusion of his remarks yesterday. Should peace come in Korea can the people of Canada expect a reduction in defence expenditures? That is important.
In conclusion may I mention one or two things in respect to a broader international policy involving defence. The hon. member for Temiscouata this afternoon indicated that he was interested in any defence policy having to do with the defence of Canada proper. I fancy that what he intended to convey was that he was not particularly in favour of vast expenditures for defence in other parts of the world. Perhaps I did not interpret him correctly, but that was the impression I received. I am not going to comment on that except to say that I believe Canada's voice should be stronger when it comes to the determination of foreign policy affecting our defence efforts abroad. We are all aware, and it is coming to light now, that in the recent past we have had nothing whatsoever to do with certain secret agreements that have been struck by the leaders of some nations, and particularly of one other great world power.
That just is not good enough. If we are to be called upon to support armies, navies and air forces against what might appear to be an aggressor, then we should demand to be heard in respect of agreements that might be struck behind the scenes. That has not been our experience in the past. We were not consulted with respect to the policy of turning Manchuria over to the Soviet, and not only turning Manchuria over to them but with
[Mr. Hansell.l

Manchuria millions and millions of dollars worth of excellent war equipment, which the Russians eventually turned over to the Mao communist administration of China to handle, and which became the base of their operations in the present struggle in Korea. We were never consulted about that, yet we are called upon to share in paying the bill.
We were never consulted in respect of the reversal of United States policy in China, which was largely responsible for communism taking over there. Some of these things, in my belief, were blunders on the part of a very large world power; but when trouble comes of course we are asked to help overcome that trouble by taking part in a shooting war. I repeat, that is not just good enough. I do not know to what extent we were called upon to enter into a discussion on whether or not General MacArthur should have been withdrawn from that scene, a man who to my mind knew the score in respect of oriental policy, if I might put it that way, at least policy in China and Japan. I do not know whether we were called in for consultation about these things or not, but we should have been. At least if we were not, then we would have a perfect right to say: well, we are not going to send men over to give their lives for what might be the protection of the blunders of others, whose blunders have been made in secret.
I do not know what is going to happen ^s a result of the present Korean struggle. I do not know if anybody else does. Whether it is going to wind up eventually with the 38th parallel being the line separating communist North Korea from Syngman Rhee's regime in South Korea, I do not know. I do not know whether it is going to result in communism boring from within in South Korea and getting all they want anyway. I do not know and perhaps nobody else knows, either.
Those are broad policies that we have to look at. We do not know what is going to result, even in Japan. We do not know whether communism may or may not bore in there and thus cause us to lose the position we once occupied, at least in the East. We do not know what is going to happen in India and other countries. I realize that these are broad matters and that someone has to make decisions. What I am saying is that when decisions in respect to these things are made we should be brought into consultation and not expected just to help fight a war, to give the lives of our young men and to give our money in order to protect the ultimate result of someone else's blunders.

Most likely the minister will be replying to the speeches that have been made and answering the questions that have been asked, and I wonder if he would answer one or two that I want to put to him. What policy does the government expect to pursue in case peace should be achieved in Korea? Are we to expect such vast expenditures to continue? Does the government regard the present Soviet move as one intended to bring about normal peace among the nations of the world, thus eliminating the necessity for such vast expenditures and bringing about a depression? What policies are the government going to pursue to prevent such depression and the making of the western nations breeding grounds for communism?
There is another question I believe the minister should answer. How much in dollars has Canada contributed toward the Korean war? That may be a little hard to determine, although it should not be too difficult. It may involve some actuarial figuring, because we know that as we carry on the training of men, as we erect various buildings necessary for the defence of Canada, as we bring into being schools and barracks and air runs, and as we provide equipment of one kind and another, these are general defence expenditures and it cannot be said just what part is for the Korean effort. But I think we should be able to arrive at some sort of comparable estimate. I repeat that I would like the minister to say just how much the Korean war has cost the taxpayers of Canada.
That is all I want to say at the present time, but I repeat that we must be careful in respect to broad international policies which involve Canada, and in connection with decisions made by other powers.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am sorry the minister is not in his seat, but probably the associate minister will be able to answer the questions which I shall bring up and which I think are fairly fundamental to our whole defence policy.
It appears from the white paper and everything that has been said by the minister and the other spokesmen for the defence department that Canada's role is to build a purely defensive force. For instance, in the air we are building fighters and interceptors, but the R.C.A.F. is to have no bombers. At sea we have anti-submarine vessels, there is a new aircraft carrier to come, we have two old cruisers, but no submarines. In the army we have a military force which has a
Supply-National Defence very low percentage of armour. The question is:	Why not bombers? Why not submarines? Why not more armour? I shall discuss that in more detail in a minute.
I realize that defence production and the production of arms is dependent entirely upon the national economy. If we use too much of the national effort to produce arms we put our economy in unbalance. A well-rounded defence force, however, must have strike-back weapons; it must have some weapons of offence. There are two ways to destroy a bomber. One is to shoot it down when it is attacking your target, and the other is to destroy the plant that makes the bomber before that bomber can attack your target.
I realize that this is a problem of some magnitude and that probably a compromise decision must be made, but it seems to me that with the history of the R.C.A.F. and the ability we showed in bombing during world war II, and considering the time that it takes to train a bomber crew, let alone a bomber wing we should now be at least training bomber personnel. All this is something to which consideration must be given at the present time. Study must also be given to the resultant effect upon technical manpower. But it seems to me that to have your air force composed entirely of fighters and interceptors, with trainers of course, is to have an air force which is in unbalance. Naturally the main problem is the defence of Canada and undoubtedly we should concentrate on interceptors and fighters, but to ignore entirely the bombing arm is, I think, open to question.
I come now to the matter of the provision of a striking naval arm which we are building so many ships to combat. I refer to the submarine. The same firm, Canadair, that is building Sabre jets and the other fighters which I shall deal with in a minute is also producing submarines. It is probably the world's premier submarine-producing firm. I refer to the Electric Boat division of the General Dynamics Corporation. The first atomic submarine cost the firm $19 million. I happen to be a shareholder of the firm because I was interested in national defence and what they were doing. In their report they have stated that the first atomic submarine cost approximately $19 million.
With a company that is already building submarines and with quite a considerable naval construction industry within our boundaries, surely there is some argument that we, whose life depends on an anti-submarine navy, should give some consideration to the advisability of the construction of submarines, particularly as we have a liaison with
3914	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence this corporation which is building Sabre jets. Modern naval thought is that a submarine is the best defence against itself.
The minister may say that the construction of this type of vessel is entirely beyond our means. I should like to point out that this firm is not only building two atomic submarines but built three new high speed submarines for the . United States last year as well as two target submarines, and has also built two large guppy submarines, the Tiburon and the Lobo, for the republic of Peru. Surely if a small country like Peru considers that the submarine is not beyond the capabilities of the country, some consideration should be given to the matter by Canada where the question of building an anti-submarine navy is of such paramount importance not only to us but to the whole free world.
Coming now to the question of the provision of armour for the military side of our defence forces, that has been dealt with before; but I feel that the more we can develop the army into an armoured force the more effective it is going to be. We can never have a large army. Our manpower precludes that, but because of our national characteristics and the mechanical ability of the Canadian people we have a flair for the production of armour and the utilization of armour in combat. I feel that the ratio of armoured to non-armoured troops should be increased in favour of armoured.
Considering the most important question of all, the function of the R.C.A.F. in the design and production of aircraft, the R.C.A.F. is a fighting service. Its primary duty is to fight. To ask a fighting service to superintend the construction and design of aircraft is to ask it to step out of its role. Not only do you not have trained engineering officers in a fighting service, but because of the rotation of officers you do not get the permanency which is required when you go into something like the production of fighter aircraft. I commend that some consideration should be given, and some discussion should take place in the house, as to the possibility of setting up a similar establishment to the ministry of supply of the United Kingdom to which technical officers are seconded from the R.A.F. Together with engineer officers you have business people with the business knowhow who deal with the problems of supply and the production of aircraft. I think that the lead the United Kingdom has today in new types of aircraft is better evidence than any that I can give of the effectiveness of this procedure.
Dealing quite briefly with Canadian production, the Canadair annual statement, which


has come to hand today, shows that they completed 453 F-86E Sabre jet fighter planes for the Canadian government in 1952. They received an order for 300 to 400 Sabre jet fighters from the British Royal Air Force. They completed the first of more than 500 T-33 Silver Star two-seater jet trainer planes for the R.C.A.F., and they prepared for the production of T-36 defence trainer transports with piston engines for the United States air force. I mention that because there you have a private company, a company with shareholders, with, I submit, a very satisfactory record in the last year so far as the production of aircraft is concerned. If nothing else shows the importance of the government divesting itself of interference with the aircraft industry, the statement of the Canadair corporation certainly does.
I will deal quite briefly with the situation at Avro. The problem of designing and producing a prototype of an entirely new aircraft, which the CF-100 is in its various marks up to the Mark 4, and producing in quantity and delivering to the service does not seem to be understood. As has been stated, the designing of the CF-100 commenced in 1947. The time to flight of the first prototype was 33 months. The time for the second prototype was 39 months. The time to delivery of first production after that was 22 months, and the time to series production in quantity and delivery to the R.C.A.F. was approximately six years. For a new aircraft, from the drawing board and with new engines, I contend, Mr. Chairman, that that is a very creditable performance and one of which we should be extremely proud. The hold-up in production of the CF-100 has been the interference of the government with the A. V. Roe Company and the system by which the R.C.A.F. controls design and interferes with the production of the aircraft right the way through. I suggest that even these figures would have been greatly improved if some mechanism similar to the United Kingdom ministry of supply had been in force in Canada. I earnestly ask the minister to comment upon that.
I want now to say something about subclause 141 on page 26 of the white paper. It is the last sentence discussing the CF-100, and it reads:
On the other hand, funds expended for aircraft development in Canada support and encourage Canadian design and development organizations, essential to the growth of the Canadian aircraft industry.
I wish the cabinet would read that sentence every day. There is nothing more important to the development of this country than that we should have our own design and our own

aircraft industry. To allow the aircraft design team, or call it what you will, at the A. V. Roe Company to be disbanded or to fall into disuse would be nothing short of criminal. I say that because of bitter experience at the outbreak of the last war. We had in Canada no aircraft industry and no people competent to design aircraft, so we were fobbed off by the United Kingdom-the United States was not in it then but the United Kingdom was- with the production of obsolete or obsolescent types of aircraft, because the United Kingdom manufacturers did not believe that it was within the competence of Canada to produce aircraft. I remember very well the hon. member for Quebec South calling me a fifth columnist, when I made my maiden speech in this house some 14 years ago, because I said that we were being fobbed off and asked to produce obsolete and obsolescent aircraft.
Mr. Chairman, we can never be put in that position again. We must have an aircraft design organization and an aircraft development organization in Canada that will keep us up in the very forefront of aircraft production. Not only is that good national defence, but it is good economics. It is a matter of dollars and cents. The cost of design for the CF-100, that is design and development costs to date, runs somewhere under $12 million, dating from 1947 to the present time, 1953. On the total order for the CF-100, up to the Mark 4 which they are now about to produce, that amounts to about $13,000 per aircraft.	[DOT]
Well, Mr. Chairman, I have looked through the report of the General Dynamics; and for licence fees to produce the Sabre jet, and patent fees and royalties which we have to pay to produce an American-designed aircraft, as far as I can find out the figure will run to very nearly $20,000 an aircraft. That figure covers all of the patent fees and all of the licences and other things concerned. It is money that is first of all lost to Canada, and which pays no taxes. Second, it is money that goes elsewhere to build up the design and development facilities of someone else's aircraft industry. I contend, Mr. Chairman, that it is not only bad business but it is bad national defence in every way. Today we have the Avro firm with the results they have produced, with a keen and alive team, and we must allow this teamwork and development to go on. We must act at once, and in this connection I would hope that there would be an immediate announcement that the production of the new aircraft, the CF-104, which I shall call the Orca, should be proceeded with immediately.
Supply-National Defence
We have seen that the life of an aircraft is limited in years. What the continuous life of the Sabre will be we do not know. We do not know when the Sabre will be replaced by the turbo-jet, but it will be replaced; and we know that the Sabre has only a certain number of years of useful life ahead of it. We also know that the CF-100 has only a certain number of useful years of combat life ahead of it. We have a limited amount of time, not much, and I contend that the CF-104 should be given the green light and proceeded with at once.
I want to quote some figures to give an example of what the United Kingdom aircraft industry is spending on development. The United Kingdom is spending some $160 million in the year 1952-53 for aeronautical design and development; and the research establishments are spending $70 million. The United Kingdom, with a frightfully heavy tax burden and shortage of materials, considers it desirable to spend money in these large amounts for research and development alone. Surely the comparatively modest amount which it will cost to develop our own aircraft in Canada should be willingly and gladly spent. The amount that it will cost to carry this on is quite modest. I have heard that the figure will be something between $5 million and $10 million a year. Mr. Chairman, we can never again fall back on someone else's design of aircraft.
In this regard I wish to disagree completely and absolutely with the statement made by the hon. member for Moose Jaw. It is bad national defence to do so, and not only that; it is bad economics. We cannot allow our engineering brains to leave this country and develop the aircraft industry in another country.

speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we are not only dealing with the department of government which asks for by far the largest sum of money from the taxpayers of Canada through their representatives now meeting here; we are also dealing with a subject which is of most vital concern to every Canadian at this time.
Yesterday a very distinguished soldier, with the widest experience of any officer in Canada today, placed on the record a clear and unchallengeable analysis of the failure of the Department of National Defence to provide national defence for Canada. The hon. member for Nanaimo has, in his own service, embraced not only the different ranks of military service but the different problems of military service in a way which I believe is unequalled by any other single officer in this country. Out of that great experience he
3916	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence has given us an analysis of the present situation. No white paper, no generalities, no interjections about equipment being designed for NATO, constitute an answer to that analysis of our defence which calls for action, not by the Minister of National Defence but by the government of Canada.
My remarks this afternoon are not directed to any one minister. They are directed to the government of Canada which is responsible for this shocking failure which has been exposed in terms that cannot be denied. Let us see exactly what the government itself declares to be the purpose of our defence objectives. These are stated on page 5 of the white paper issued the day before yesterday under the title "Canada's Defence Program." Under the heading "Canada's Defence Objectives", we read the following:
The objectives of our defence policy remain the same as heretofore:
(1)	The immediate defence of Canada and North America from direct attack;
(2)	implementation of any undertakings made by Canada under the charter of the United Nations, or under the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, or other agreement for collective security;
(3)	the organization to build up strength in a total war.
Mr. Chairman, those are the objectives as declared by the government. Surely, therefore, it is appropriate that we should examine what the result has been from the expenditure of over $5 billion since the end of the war, and more than $4 billion since the beginning of the period which commenced with the act of aggression in Korea.
Let us deal with the second item first. In so far as the implementation of any undertakings made by Canada under the charter of the United Nations or under the North Atlantic Treaty Organization or other agreement for collective security is concerned, we must, in a very large measure, accept the statement of the government without too complete information as to the details. Those who have already spoken have indicated their own admiration for the high standard of efficiency displayed by these young men in uniform who are taking part in the various duties which constitute the implementation of these various agreements. Every Canadian shares the pride that is the proper appreciation of the gallant and courageous action of our young men in the different units serving in Korea. Those who have seen their services, and those who have seen the other units now outside of Canada, have expressed their admiration for the way in which those young men are taking their part in the various operations that are part of our attempt to defend freedom by a plan of collective security.


I have seen the Canadian troops in Europe. They are giving Canadians the same reason for pride that Canadians have given in other places where the Canadian uniform is worn. I have seen the Canadian squadrons in Europe. I have seen the operations of those squadrons, and I have also had reason to know something of the admiration that is expressed for those young men who fly the aircraft which have gone from Canada to Europe. I have seen something of our naval forces, and I know the splendid job they are doing. It is because our young men and young women in uniform are always capable of giving a good account of themselves, and adding new reasons for pride in the name of Canada which they carry on their shoulders, that we should recognize the extent to which many young Canadians today, both men and women, are being denied the opportunity to give the kind of service they want to give by the failure of this government to fulfil its own undertakings in regard to the defence of this country.
Nothing that is said here can be interpreted as any reflection on the young men and women of Canada, either in uniform or out of it. It is because we know how good they are that we have a right and a duty to examine what the situation really is, and what the facts are in regard to the defence of this country at this time.
I have referred to the second item of our defence objectives, and I say that to the extent that we know wh#t is being done, we certainly have reason for pride in the achievements and conduct of the young Canadians who have gone from Canada or are training in Canada to fulfil our obligations under the charter of the United Nations, the North Atlantic Treaty Organization or other agreements for collective security.
But then let us examine the other two. Let us remember that we are told that the first objective is the immediate defence of Canada and North America from direct attack. The hon. member for Nanaimo yesterday pointed out-and gave supporting figures- that in spite of this tremendous expenditure the government has not provided for the defence of Canada and North America from direct attack. In fact the hon. member for Nanaimo has made it clear that not one service-the army, the navy or the air force -in so far as the direct defence of Canada is concerned, is in a position to meet an attack of that kind.
Then also there is the other item under Canada's defence objectives: the organization to build up strength in total war. The statements made by the hon. member for Nanaimo

and by other hon. members who spoke yesterday and today have made it perfectly clear that we have not today the organization to build up strength in total war or otherwise.
Mr. Chairman, the defence of Canada against the possibility of direct attack simply does not exist. With all the fine spirit of those who seek to serve, our naval defence is inadequate for that purpose; our air defence is non-existent; and the army defence is wholly ineffective for that task because of the limitation upon mobility and the lack of equipment to which reference has already been made.
I think some further reference should be made to our reserve forces. At all times it has been recognized that in this country the reserve forces are the backbone of our defence. We never at any time have pretended that our permanent forces are adequate in peacetime for the defence of Canada. It is to the reserves that we look for the larger numbers . and the possibility of expansion. That has been the case through long years of the military history of Canada. Today the reserve force is simply not being allowed to fulfil its allotted task; and that statement applies to every branch of the reserve forces.
Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to go through one unit after another in order to indicate the situation with which the reserve units of this country are confronted at this time.
I wish, however, to refer to an interjection made by the Minister of National Defence yesterday when, in reply to a statement by the hon. member for Calgary East, as reported at page 3833 of Hansard, he said:
The hon. member must know that the equipment to which he refers is being taken away to be rehabilitated and then shipped to Europe, and will be replaced by equipment of the latest type. That procedure is well under way.
I wish to speak about that interjection, because it referred to a statement that arms and equipment had been taken away from certain reserve units and that they were incapable of performing their responsibilities. The answer given by the Minister of National Defence is not in keeping with the understanding of the reserve units which find themselves in that position.
It is by giving specific illustrations that the general situation can best be understood. Let me give the example of one artillery regiment. I am under the impression that the figures I give in this case will be found to be repeated generally in the case of other artillery regiments across Canada. I will give the figures in regard to an artillery regiment of three batteries. It happens to be one of the oldest artillery regiments in Canada, with a record of efficiency which
Supply-National Defence indicates why it is certainly a perfectly fair test of the present situation.
That regiment, in addition to its headquarters, has three batteries authorized. Two of those batteries are at present activated. The number of guns required for three batteries of that type is 32 for that regiment. That regiment at present has four guns instead of 32. A year ago it had eight. Four were taken away. The four that remain cannot be fired. In fact they cannot even give effective training with the four guns they have, because not one of those four guns has a breech-block. Everyone with any knowledge of gunnery training knows that, without a breech-block, you cannot give effective training in loading and firing guns.
Last year it was decided that the breech rings on the guns needed to be changed. The regiment was informed that these guns could not be fired. Four of the guns were taken away, not with any explanation that they were to be sent to NATO but with the explanation that they were to have the breech rings replaced, and with the understanding that the guns would then be available for firing practice. The other four guns remained, but they could not be used for firing. As far as that is concerned, they could not give the members of the battery effective training anyway, because the tractors that haul these guns are not adequate for the job. Therefore even if they could give effective gun drill, they cannot train the men for the camp to which they are expected to go during the coming summer in this very critical period.
Up to a month ago they had eight gun tractors. Five were taken away. Now they have only three tractors. The jeeps were taken away a year ago, with the understanding that they were to be replaced; but they have not been replaced. The fact is that this artillery regiment, which certainly can be shown to be one of the better artillery regiments in Canada, is worse off from the point of view of equipment than it has been at any time since the war. To my knowledge it is worse off than it has been at any time either since the last war or in between the two world wars. That is the situation with which we find ourselves confronted after $5 billion has been spent for defence.

I shall be very happy to let the Minister of National Defence know the name of the regiment, and I shall do it outside of the house. I have no doubt he is aware that

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
I shall be very happy to let him know the name of the regiment. The minister is aware that I have not completely severed my association with the artillery.
The situation is this. These units are trying to train gunners without serviceable guns. They are trying to train gunners for camp this summer in what we are told is a very critical period without the opportunity to give them adequate tactical manoeuvres. These units cannot even do what are described as dry exercises, under which the gunners could be given some impression of what their duties will be in camp. Nor are those who will be charged with the responsibility for handling the movement of the vehicles being given the type of training that will qualify them to perform that task when they go to camp. As everyone knows, whether they have been with one service or another, it is not simply a case of getting onto a tractor and then moving that tractor. There are involved movements by signal which call for a great deal of training. The officers of these units, when they are carrying out their exercises in preparation for camp, are called upon to use their own automobiles for that purpose. They are using their own private cars for command post training.
I have not given these figures, Mr. Chairman, with the idea that this is an isolated case. It is not. Right across Canada units find themselves in a similar position today in varying degrees. If a reason is sought for the inability to maintain the enlistment level of our reserve units, it will be found in the atmosphere of utter unreality which is created by the shortage of weapons and equipment in the reserve units of this country at this time. That remark applies to other branches of the army as well as the artillery.
It is extremely difficult to get young men, keen young men, anxious to perform some useful task, to go through the movements of drill when they know that what they are doing has little relation to the kind of training they will be called upon to do in camp. If this were a period in which we had been spending little money then of course one might understand and even seek to justify a situation of this kind. How is it possible to justify a situation of this kind after an expenditure of $5 billion? There can be no justification. If our present results are to be the measure of what we get for $5 billion, then think of what would happen to Canada if by any unhappy chance we were called upon really to take part in war. God forbid 
that that should happen, but there is no sensible person who does not realize that this training is done with the knowledge that the dreadful possibility of war is always there.
If what we have now received for the expenditure of $5 billion is to be the measure of the result of such expenditure, then this country would literally almost bankrupt itself if it were called upon to raise the forces that we might be called upon to raise with the serious threat of a more imminent emergency than that which now confronts us. These figures, this expenditure of $5 billion and the inadequate results flowing from that expenditure, indicate why this parliament and the people of Canada should have assurances which have not yet been given to them.
I hope no one is going to imagine that after the consideration of these estimates we are going to know very much more about the ' details than we know now. We have learned by experience that this government will use its majority at any time to close the door upon information that we are seeking. We do know that there has been waste, extravagance and inefficiency of the most astounding kind. We know that from the very small measure of information which has come to us as a result of inquiries which have been conducted. We know that within the very limited area of the inquiries which have actually taken place waste, extravagance, and inefficiency give a very clear indication of why we have these inadequate results after the enormous expenditure of money which has taken place.
Effort after effort has been made to have a complete and exhaustive inquiry into the whole organization and administration of the Department of National Defence, which was found to be inefficient by the one impartial inquiry which has gone into the administration of that department and which we have been permitted to examine. Statements made within the last few days, Mr. Chairman, have not been reassuring. In the white paper tabled the day before yesterday we find this statement:
During 1952-53, in addition to meeting its own requirements, Canada was able to sell a number of F-86E Sabre aircraft to the United States for successful operation in Korea.
Then in Hansard of yesterday, the following day, we find the minister giving us information in the following words, as reported at page 3809:
We have deliberately postponed the equipping of our own forces with additional Sabre fighters in order to make Sabres available to the United States and to Britain.

There are several clear inconsistencies between the white paper which was tabled the day before yesterday and the statements made yesterday by the minister, and there are inconsistencies as between the various white papers. But these are not things which call for our attention to the same extent as the simple fact that after the expenditure of more than $5,000 million the reserve forces of this country are incapable of performing the tasks allotted to them and of meeting the test laid down by the government itself in regard to those defence forces.
We also have the fact, and it is an alarming fact, that in spite of these enormous expenditures our defence forces are not capable of undertaking the immediate defence of Canada from direct attack. That is the first objective of our defence preparations as declared by the government itself. The government has already spent $5,000 million and asks for more than $2,000 million more without having gone very far toward meeting that first requirement, according to its own statement.
Nor have we met the requirement stated by the government of an organization to build up strength in total war. We know that one of the ways in which we can most likely hope to prevent war is to have it known by Russia that there is in Canada as in the other free nations an organization capable of building up the strength of the defence forces beyond those now in existence. Those requirements have not been met. It is a story of failure for which this government has given no effective answer.
I repeat that my remarks are not directed to the Minister of National Defence; my remarks are directed to the Prime Minister and government of Canada. This is their responsibility. They are asking the people of Canada to provide this year more than $2,000 million on top of more than $5,000 million already spent. We should have and the people of Canada should have at this stage assurance by the Prime Minister on behalf of the government that in the face of these admitted inadequacies there will be an immediate, effective and complete inquiry into the administration, organization and general activities of the Department of National Defence.
We are not going to be able to change this situation during the course of the discussion of these money items now before us. We know perfectly well, having regard to the policy of the government, that we are not to know very much more after these estimates have been dealt with than we know now as to what the results are going to be. Let anyone outside of this house who suggests that the opposition could have obtained more
Supply-National Defence information than they did remember that the government has denied an opportunity to obtain information in the one effective way in which it could be obtained. It was effective in that limited case where less than one per cent of the expenditures was under examination. We have sought a similarly effective examination in regard to the total expenditures of the department.
Recognizing that we cannot obtain the facts from a government which uses its majority to deny the facts, I urge that the Prime Minister on behalf of the whole government reassure this house at this time and reassure the people of Canada, who now learn that they have not the defence they had the right to expect, that there will be a review of the organization, administration and accounting of the Department of National Defence as a result of which we may expect to get results from the money that we are called upon to spend.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the Leader of the Opposition in his opening remarks properly gave praise to the personnel of the Canadian forces in the Far East and in Europe. He did that under the head of speaking about the second objective of our national defence, namely the implementation of any undertakings made by Canada under the charter of the United Nations or under the North Atlantic treaty or other agreements for collective security.
If I understood him aright, the Leader of the Opposition said that with the information available he felt that in this respect we were doing what we said we were doing. That is all right. There are three objectives in our national defence which we have set out. The first is the defence of Canada against immediate attack. The third is to enable us to mobilize our resources to meet an all-out objective. The ' second, at this time of cold war and of activities in Korea and of the building up of the strength of the North Atlantic treaty nations in Europe, is really part of the other two.
Who is to say which should come first. In the view of the government they are all part of the single problem of national defence. They are aspects of one thing that has to be done. We must take our part in the cold war and at the same time be prepared for a hot war should it come.
In his speech the Leader of the Opposition praised our soldiers and by necessary implication acknowledged the part played by the government, by the department and by the armed forces in respect to that very important second category, carrying out our commitments to the United Nations in Korea

Supply-National Defence and to the North Atlantic Treaty Organization in Europe. This is the first time in six years that the Leader of the Opposition has made such an acknowledgment. If he stays on that side and we stay on this side of the house, as we all expect will be the case for some time further, it may be that he will be in a position next year or perhaps the following year to acknowledge that we have done equally well on the first and third points, because we are just on the way to getting there.
The building up of our armed forces at the rate at which ii has been done has been, as we all know, a large job, and it has been a complicated one. In his remarks the Leader of the Opposition made several sweeping assertions, but he based his whole case largely upon the analysis that had been made by the hon. member for Nanaimo. I propose, in replying to hon. members who have taken part in the debate so far, dealing with as many points as I can and answering such questions as I can without delaying the house too long, to begin by taking up the remarks of the hon. member for Nanaimo.
He said in his speech yesterday, if you remember, that our one and only aircraft carrier, H.M.C.S. Magnificent, is the only vessel of her class which to date has not been modernized. My information is that that is not the case and that so far only one vessel of the class to which the Magnificent belongs is in process of modernization. He also said, as found at page 3815 of Hansard:
* . . only the prototype of the new anti-submarine escort ship has so far been commissioned. She is the former destroyer H.M.C.S. Algonquin . . .
The Algonquin is not the prototype of the new anti-submarine escort vessel. She is the first of our Tribal class destroyers to be modernized and equipped with mess decks, bunks, new electronic and fire control apparatus and the like. She is not one of the new anti-submarine escort vessels. The hon. member also said:
There are fourteen destroyer escorts of Canadian design and fourteen coastal minesweepers being built in Canadian yards. Of the former, I understand that nine keels only have been laid to date.
Nine keels have been laid, but with modern shipbuilding practice that is not necessarily a good indication of the degree of progress, because so much is done in different parts of the whole operation. Three of these ships have been launched. All fourteen of the coastal minesweepers have been launched, and we expect that they will be completed during this fiscal year. The hon. member for Nanaimo went on to say:
In reserve we have a wartime fleet of frigates and minesweepers. If they are to be used, they 

must be completely modernized before they could possibly fulfil any of their roles in the event of an emergency.
All of these ships in reserve will, we expect, be modernized in the present fiscal year. Some of them already have been, and the work is well in hand. Then the hon. member remarked on the fact that we had no submarines, which of course is self-evident. But it would be spreading our resources very thinly indeed if, in addition to going in for an aircraft carrier, we went in for a submarine as well and had an orphan submarine. It is much better for us to go along with the arrangement we have with the Royal Navy and the United States navy to borrow a submarine for training purposes whenever we need it.
Then the hon. member came to his remarks on the army. He referred at some length to the position of the striking or mobile airborne force for the direct defence of Canada. It seems to me that he has been badly misinformed about the situation of the mobile striking force. This force exists now and includes the second battalions of the three regiments. The required number of men to make it effective for the purpose for which it is designed have been trained. In addition to the infantry units there are units of artillery, engineers, army service corps, signals, medicals, and so on, who are also trained airborne troops.
Then he suggested that we should have special engineers trained to make airfields, apparently after they had landed. This is not according to the concept of defence that my advisers have. Indeed, in the operations in which we have engaged in training and in working out the doctrine of defence of our north, the fewer airfields we have the fewer airfields we have to defend against the possibility of the enemy using them as steppingstones from which to leapfrog toward our settled1 areas. Indeed, were it possible the greatest single defence throughout our northland would be the rough nature of the ground and the extent of the territory itself.
We recall, for example, how important were the 21 miles of the channel even during the period of the bomber and fighter attack. There is a depth of a good deal more than 2,000 miles in our northland, and this would be very useful indeed. The concept of this defence is that with the equipment that the only potential enemy has he cannot make a large-scale airborne attack and landing in force on this continent at the present time, and we have arranged with our United States allies that each of us shall have the force which we together have agreed upon to be

desirable to clean up any operation that we would anticipate might take place in the future so far as we can foresee it. We have that force; we have it now.
What is more, we have the transport to enable that force to be used. Hon. members have referred to the fact that hitherto we have only had Dakotas to use for this operation, and very good they were too. A good many countries in the world still only have Dakotas, but to them we have added a number of C-119's. They are coming along at the rate of several per month. Therefore we believe that today we have an airlift sufficient to meet the kind of situation envisaged by the concept on which we are working. Exercises are held regularly. Parts of these formations are trained in succession in winter warfare at Churchill and in airborne operations at other places. Last year a large exercise was held at Churchill. Another exercise, exercise Bulldog, was held at Norman Wells. The airstrip was defended by a force acting the part of an enemy, and was then retaken by an airborne force. Similar exercises have been held at Wain-wright, Fort Chimo and other places. There are usually two such planned each year.
In addition, our officers are being trained steadily both in the doctrine and management of these operations. At Rivers there is the joint airborne training school operated for the benefit of the navy, army and air force. There, three weeks ago I was present at the closing lecture to the army staff college and the air staff college. It was attended by representatives of ten different countries, including a very large team from the United States. They all had spent over ten days at Rivers and elsewhere working over specific plans for just this kind of operation. In fact at the staff colleges, as well as in training exercises for both army and air force, this has formed a major part of their training over the last several years.
Then the hon. member referred to antiaircraft artillery. On that I was very frank. There is not in the world today any antiaircraft artillery of the conventional type or of new type which is really adequate to deal with fast high-flying jets. Fortunately, we do not know that the only potential enemy has any such jets that can reach this continent carrying a load of bombs; but on the other hand we do have in Canada anti-aircraft guns of the latest conventional type and we are modifying them so as to make them just as effective as conventional antiaircraft guns can be made. We are not going to go into a complete outfitting of all our own forces, active and reserve, at an expenditure of something like $500,000 per
Supply-National Defence gun, with weapons which will unquestionably be rendered obsolete within a period of 3, 4 or 5 years. In the meantime we have a considerable number of the latest types of guns. They are being modified with the latest types of devices, and there is nothing better than those of which we know. All we could do would be to get more of those, if they existed, and have them delivered to us at just about the time when we are rather confident that there will be a far more effective weapon in production in the form of ground-to-air guided missiles.
The hon. member referred again to the 27th brigade and expressed the thought which he has so often expressed, that we should have more armour. I have gone into that before, and I do not think there is any point in repeating the observations I have made on previous occasions. We have the type of unit we were asked to provide and which fits into the scheme of things on the other side. It enables us to train and operate independently as a unit, but an independent armoured brigade group working in isolation from a division or a group, as I have said before, is a military monstrosity. We have never heard of such an organization, and it could not operate.
What would have to be done to carry out the suggestions as I understand them would be to add elements to our infantry brigade group to constitute a balanced force of very considerable proportions. Well, we have no intention whatever of increasing our manpower commitments on the other side at the present time. From the studies I have made and that I have had made for me, we feel that to carry out this suggestion would not mean a saving in manpower; for in order to create the unit that has been suggested, as we understand it, we would require larger forces than the present ones.
With regard to the tanks used by the 27th brigade, the hon. member referred to the fact that a number of Centurion tanks had been issued to the squadron. He said:
It is a start in the right direction, the direction which I recommended.
I am sorry but I cannot give him that satisfaction, because the squadron had tanks before the suggestion was made by the hon. member. It had Sherman tanks with which it was outfitted on this side and, as soon as they became available, we replaced the Shermans with Centurions for several reasons, the main one being maintenance on the other side. Also the Centurion is more modern and in some ways, but not all, a more effective tank for Europe than the Sherman.
Then the hon. member said:
-it is highly questionable whether they

Supply-National Defence -the aircraftare of types suitable for the work for which they were intended.
As far as my advisers tell me, and that means the chief of the air staff and his technical officers, the aircraft we have and that we are getting are the aircraft best suited for the purpose for which we are getting them. If the hon. member has in mind one type, namely the Lancasters which we have modified for use as maritime reconnaissance aircraft, then I can tell him that we do not know of any other aircraft in the world today more suitable for this type of work over the waters over which our aircraft have to travel. There is not one. We have had to make these modifications and we have done so, because it was the cheapest way of going about it. Otherwise it would have been necessary to design and build a new long-range aircraft.
The Lancasters will, of course, wear out and they will have to be replaced; and we are looking into the question of what is to be the ultimate replacement of the Lancaster for maritime reconnaissance. So far we have not found the answer. We do not know that such an aircraft is yet on the design board of any country. We do not want to have to go ourselves into the design of a fundamentally new type of aircraft if we can get one from another country which can possibly be modified, adapted and built in this country or purchased from abroad. The Lancaster is the only aircraft to which the hon. member's remarks could be directed, I should think, and the answer is as I have stated.
We are producing the F-86E, the CF-100, the T-33 trainer, the latest Harvard type trainer, plus light transport aircraft-the Otter, the Beaver and the Chipmunk, leading aircraft of their type. As far as we know there is not anything to match them; and it is high time, I think, that the Canadian people began to recognize that their air force has become one of the leading air forces in effective fighting power on our side today.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
When the committee rose I was dealing with some of the points made by the hon. member for Nanaimo. There is one more that I should mention. He referred to the nine auxiliary fighter squadrons distributed throughout the length and breadth of Canada from Montreal to Vancouver, "which are equipped," as he said "with world war II


Mustangs and more or less worn-out British-built Vampires". The situation regarding those I have already described. It does happen that for the type of air attack which might be made on Canada and North America, with the type of aircraft which the only possible enemy are believed to have with the capacity to carry a bomb load to this continent, world war II Mustangs and Vampires would be, not the best defence, but a very good defence. They are the kind of planes that dealt with this kind of aircraft during the war, and which a number of other countries have to deal with today.
The fact is that had we obtained other types of aircraft to replace the Mustangs and Vampires we would have been using our resources on aircraft that would soon have become obsolete, instead of which we decided, as a matter of deliberate policy, to go for the F-86E for its particular role of fighter interceptor and the CF-100 for its role of long range, all-weather fighter. The CF-100 was designed for the defence of Canada, and the F-86E was not. While the F-86E is unquestionably the leading aircraft of its type in the world today, it by no means follows that that is the ideal type of aircraft for the kind of operation we envisage as being necessary to defend Canada in the next few years. The range of this aircraft is not great, it has not full instrumentation and does not carry a navigator. Consequently anyone familiar with flying conditions in our north country would recognize that, while the F-88E would give a good account of itself, the losses would be high due to the fact that it might not be able to get back to its base again. We therefore went for the CF-100, designed particularly for the purpose, and so far as we know it is the best aircraft to meet that purpose.
What is important from the point of view of this committee is to recognize that there was no alternative to following this course. So far as we know there is not a long-range allweather fighter in production anywhere comparable to the CF-100, and designed to meet conditions as we envisage likely to obtain in the next few years on this continent. In the meantime these Vampires and Mustangs have proven very worthy against the only type of bomber that we know the enemy has in quantities able to deliver a bomb load on North America.
There is quite a different problem from the one in northwestern Europe, where the main objective would be to secure command of the air by destruction of many fighters. In the defence of North America it is not envisaged at the present time that fighters from any enemy country could travel the distance required. Consequently there is an interim period during which Vampires and Mustangs

will be useful. To have acquired any other aircraft would have been wasteful, we think. The CF-100 is designed for the job.
The hon. member for Nanaimo referred to our construction program and asked what plan is being followed in respect to the erection of permanent or semi-permanent buildings. He indicated that this matter had been dealt with by the special committee on defence expenditures. It was dealt with during a series of sessions. I can refer him particularly to June 12, 1952 and March 17, 1953. This question of the type of construction, the need for it, the scale and quality of the construction was gone into by that committee at that time. Certainly in June of last year the scales and standards of construction, the way in which contracts were placed, the number of square feet per man, and all the other elements that might give hon. members an opportunity to exercise some judgment of their own, were laid before the committee. Reading the records of the committee at that time, I can see no objection being there made to them. Those scales and standards were worked out over a period of years having regard to wartime experience and having regard also to the conditions that existed in Canada, the conditions which existed in other countries and the way they have been met there.
I have not heard any hon. member specify any particular instance in respect of which the allowance has been too great for the Canadian sailor, soldier or airman. If any hon. member thought that, he might have said so. I have not heard, either, that the costs were too high, having regard to building costs throughout the country.
In all these cases, except in the few referred to in the statement by the hon. member for Halifax where there were cost-plus contracts because of special considerations, the contracts were let on tender and the buildings are there. Hon. members have been given numerous opportunities of seeing them. If they feel that they are too luxurious for the Canadian sailor, soldier, or airman, they ought to say so. In fact they ought to have said so a long time ago, because the facts on which they could have based their judgment have been before them for a long time now.
The hon. member for Cape Breton South made a speech which I think appealed to most hon. members of this committee, as do most of his speeches. He began by disclaiming any special knowledge as an expert. He said he approached this consideration with the viewpoint of an ordinary man. He expresses the view of the ordinary citizen in no ordinary fashion because he speaks from the heart, and he speaks his mind effectively and forcefully. With a great deal of his speech I was in complete agreement.
Supply-National Defence
He referred to the terms of enlistment for service in Korea and in Germany, and it seems to me that there he had been misinformed, because after the special force had been enlisted for 18 months or duration in Korea, everyone else was enlisted in the Canadian armed forces for a minimum of three years, and that procedure has been going on. Every effort is made, of course, to keep in the armed forces the men. we want to keep.
He referred to the National Defence Act as having cut down some of the rights of the service personnel. As I suggested to him, that has not been the case. What was done was to arrive at a service disciplinary code for all three services on a sound basis; and we were the first country in the world to do that. We did it after this disciplinary code had been considered by committees of the other place and of the House of Commons over a period of many months. The result has been not that the rights of the common soldier have been reduced but that they are actually greater than before.
He said that officers in the three services had long complained about the requirement that they purchase their own dress uniforms and certain items of equipment. I do not know to what that refers, but he must have had in mind the fact that all officers in all three services receive an allowance of $375 towards the purchase of their equipment: and in addition they are issued, at cost, items such as battledress, working clothes and so on.
He referred to the educational and information services. Here a considerable change has been made over the last 18 months in that we have instituted the bureau of current affairs which serves all three services with publications, booklets, wall charts and the like as well as lectures and education courses with officers and others as discussion leaders. We have communicated with our opposite numbers in the allied countries, and I think most of them would agree that we are a good deal in advance of the other countries in this respect, namely in the respect of putting before our service personnel information on which they can base their own views and which will serve as the basis of discussion. If hon. members are interested in any of this material, they can always have it. A great number have expressed interest. I must say that throughout the whole course of publications-and the publications are given out every two weeks in French and in English- I have never had a single complaint about any text or any work from any hon. member of this chamber; and they are fairly ready to voice their views if they find anything wrong along that line.

Supply-National Defence
As to education, all members of the armed forces have available to them the educational services which were conducted by the Canadian Legion and the Department of Veterans Affairs during the war and which are now continued. In addition, we have voluntary educational classes which will become compulsory with effect from September, 1953, for educational courses up to grade VIII. That system is already in effect for the 27th infantry brigade, but it is not possible to make it effective in Korea.
The next statement to which I refer is that of the hon. member for Calgary East, who made some assertions about waste and commented on how the cost of having a man in the armed forces has mounted year by year. This brings me to a point that has been made by numerous hon. members opposite, including the hon. member for Moose Jaw just before the adjournment. I think it was started in an editorial in the Globe and Mail of November 17, 1952. I refer to the procedure whereby you arrive at the cost of the soldier by dividing the number of service personnel into the total amount spent on defence for that year. I would point out that the two things bear no relation whatever.
Let us take, for example, the case of the United States or Britain and ourselves. Before the second world war Britain and the United States had large regular forces in peacetime and they had the physical equipment, the accommodation, the training facilities and the great camp areas necessary to train men. We did not. Before the beginning of the second world war we had for the armed forces in Canada virtually no special accommodation of any kind. Almost all were living in established centres. Most of them were engaged on administrative and training work. We had virtually no forces in being, to use that commonly-used expression. Consequently when, at the end of the second world war and particularly since Korea, we had to build up our forces, we had to spend much more per man simply on constructing accommodation in which he could live, as well as mess halls and the other facilities.
It may also be pointed out that in the case of both the United Kingdom and the United States they have a much larger proportion of their personnel serving abroad. In respect of those men serving in Germany, for example, all construction and all maintenance costs have so far been met out of occupation costs whereas, in the case of Canada, we pay our own maintenance costs. These comparisons are therefore invalid and misleading. If you want to get a proper basis of comparison you must find out how much is paid to each
[Mr. Claxton.l

soldier in Britain, Canada and the United States for pay and allowances, clothing, food, pension, medical and dental services, the equivalent of a civilian wage.
I have set out in my statement at page 3807 the costs for Canada. We have looked into the problem of finding similar costs in the United States and Britain. It is pretty difficult to arrive at costs because of the different way in which their figures are computed; but by and large I would say that the cost of maintaining an average service person throughout the year in Canada is not far off that in the United States. The pay and allowances in the United States are a bit higher than in Canada, corresponding in part to the difference in the wage levels in the two countries. But the cost of clothing in Canada is a bit higher than the cost of clothing a soldier, sailor or airman in the United States, owing to the difference in climate. The figures work out very closely indeed. If you take a weighted figure, having regard to the proportion of officers, N.C.O.'s and so on, you get a higher figure on a per capita basis for the United States than for Canada.
If you compare the figures by the process of division that the hon. member for Moose Jaw used, and that has been used by other hon. members, then you ought to be pretty sure that you have the same basis for comparison. That is, the total costs for Canada should be less expenditures on mutual aid, less expenditures on stockpiling, and should be on a totally comparable basis. After you arrive at that you have to consider how much more one country puts into the air force, which is much the most expensive service and how much more another country will put in the army, which is the least expensive service, on a per capita basis. So these comparisons, on a per capita cost basis, arrived at by the process of dividing the total costs of defence by the number of personnel in the armed forces, are, I suggest totally invalid and cannot stand up to any serious examination.
Then the hon. member for Calgary East referred, as several others have done, to the statement of Wing Commander Rohmer. Here I must admit I am in a little difficult position. I do not think it is necessarily desirable that I should answer in the house or in public the statements of an officer in the air force reserve. This one happens to be a man with a good record during the war. He was a flight lieutenant at the end of the war. Had he stayed on in the active forces he would toy now be at about the rank of squadron leader with about one year's seniority. However, he went into the reserve.

He became a wing commander in charge of one of the squadrons in Toronto, and I found on inquiry that he was about 275th on the list of seniority of wing commanders in the air force.

It is rather important to keep a sense of proportion. In my position I do not make decisions about air force plans, about the program of aircraft, about how many aircraft are to be sent abroad, the types of aircraft we are going to make, without long, patient and thorough investigation by the people whom I regard as the most competent in the world to make that investigation, namely my advisers and the Royal Canadian Air Force. This starts with the chief of air staff, with his long experience, and all his officers. I do not say I always take their advice, but generally I do on technical matters.
In any event, whenever a matter comes up of any important consequence involving future policies it goes to other government departments and is considered by them and by the cabinet defence committee, and is ultimately approved by the cabinet. Everyone knows that is the procedure. I do not profess to be an expert, but I should like to read to the committee a letter written by Wing Commander Rohmer to Crawford Gordon, Jr., president of A. V. Roe Canada Limited, Malton, Ontario, on February 27, 1953, before this matter came up. He wrote:
Dear Mr. Gordon:
The officers of 411	(F) squadron (auxiliary)
toured your plant last evening.
On behalf of the squadron members, I wish to thank you for the privilege of seeing the progress which your firm has made toward the ultimate high production of the CF-100.
Supply-National Defence
This progress is of special significance to us, inasmuch as the plans of the air force to date provide for our use of your aircraft at the earliest possible moment.
What we saw last night has given all of us a much better perspective as regards what we might expect by way of production and quality of production. As you are well aware, there have been several rumours and stories as to the capability and potential of A. V. Roe. It was my intention in asking for this visit to discredit in the minds of my officers that any contrary rumours that they might have heard should be dispelled.
Such is the case today, and we are looking forward with confidence to watching the CF-100 roll off the line in quantity and to flying it.
My compliments to your conducting staff, and in particular, to Mr. Jackson who handled our group with a great deal of care and attention.
Yours sincerely,
Richard H. Rohmer, W/C. Commanding Officer,
411 (F) squadron (auxiliary)

The hon. member for Calgary East then went on to talk about overblown staffs. This is the easiest kind of charge to make, of course, and it would be very easy for me to say, as I do, that this is a matter of gravest concern to all of us, to keep down our staffs to the lowest possible level so as to ensure adequate control with the least possible number of controllers.
Hon. members have referred a great deal to the Currie report, and some hon. members have heard that report discussed before the special committee on defence expenditures. They will find from the evidence that the statement I made in the house on January 13 was completely confirmed, that is that a major factor in the lack of control which gave rise to my appointing Mr. Currie and the making of his report was the lack of sufficient staff to do the job. Actually we are understaffed today in the Department of National Defence.
The hon. member went on to give as his only example of this the situation in the office of the deputy minister, and stated that there are now more personnel there than at any time during the war. The hon. member for Kamloops made the same statement and gave the same figures at page 3840 of Hansard.

The answer to this is the following figures. The present staff in the deputy minister's office is 114 as compared with totals of 98, 93 and 77 for the staffs of the three defence deputies on March 31, 1944, March 31, 1945 and March 31, 1946 respectively. The increase is due exclusively to the assumption by the present deputy minister of national defence of responsibility for several functions that were previously allotted to the services. They have been assumed either to permit a greater degree of co-ordination or control or to replace service personnel with civilians.
The chief secretary with a staff of 29 provides secretarial services for the interservices committees, an activity previously carried out by service personnel. The present arrangement has the advantage of providing greater continuity since service officers can be appointed as committee secretaries only for short periods.
Until recently each of the three services was responsible for preparing its own estimates and for a number of other financial control functions. The assistant deputy minister of defence, who came to the Department of National Defence from the Department of Finance, now co-ordinates the financial control and the preparation of estimates for all three services. The present staff of this branch is 23.
The real estate adviser's office with a staff of eight also carries out a function that until recently was performed by the three services. The controller of office services and supplies with a staff of three co-ordinates the demands of the three services for stationery supplies and office equipment. Experience has shown that substantial economies have been achieved by co-ordinating the demands for this type of supplies. Thus of the total staff of 114 in the office of the deputy minister, 64 are engaged in activities that were not undertaken by the three deputies in 1944, 1945 and 1946. So the increase in staff over the comparative figures for those years is attributable entirely to the additional functions now carried on.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE

I hope he has seen similar bundles outside every department of government and I hope, as in this case, they are sold as waste paper on tender. What else the hon. member would expect to do with it, I do not know.

Then the hon. member dealt with the question of equipment for the reserve forces, and he quoted largely from an article which had appeared in the Calgary Herald. The hon. member said:
They told me their carriers were about to be taken away from them.
I do not know where he got this information, but if it is so it must be because the carriers they had were worn out. So far there is nowhere that we know of an acceptable modern infantry carrier. Everyone on our side is working on one, but we have not found anything better. Then the hon. member said, "Their jeeps have gone already." The jeeps were removed from the reserve army units and active force units in order to renovate them and send them to Europe where they were urgently required to be used for operational training, and were immediately replaced with a new type made during the last 18 months which are now pooled under the control of the general officers commanding. Jeeps that were used previously for administrative purposes are being replaced by *commercial type vehicles. More than 80 per cent of that operation is complete, and I would think that it will all be complete this month.
The hon. member suggested that the reserve force officers should be given a tour of duty in Korea. That is provided for if they will agree to serve a year. It would not be economical on any other basis.
Then the hon. member dealt with promotions within the Royal Canadian Air Force, I understand particularly those on the administrative list. Everyone in the Royal Canadian Air Force up to the rank of squadron leader is required to take examinations in order to qualify for promotion. Above that rank it is considered that officers generally should be on the general list, but there are arrangements under way under which they can move from one to the other.

In the case of the two buildings in Montreal we see that they were sold only three and a half years later for a fifth of the amount paid for them.
