The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre referred again, as he has on numerous occasions, to the shortage of ammunition. I suggest that this is a matter on which hon. members should exercise the usual caution which should be applied to matters affecting the morale and welfare of the troops. I can read to him a statement made in the British House of Commons on March 26, 1953. The quotation is as follows:
Mr. Shinwell asked the Prime Minister, as the head of our defence forces, whether he was informed of the shortage of ammunition for United Nations troops in Korea; and what action was taken in the matter.
The Prime Minister; I am informed that the ammunition supply in Korea has always been sufficient to meet the operational requirements of the United Nations forces, and shortages of ammunition have not restricted the planning of operations.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
But has the right hon. gentleman not been informed of the statement made quite recently by General Van Fleet on his retirement from the command in Korea to the effect that there has been a considerable shortage of ammunition?
The Prime Minister; I have to rely upon the official information which is transmitted to us in due course. I cannot deal with every statement that is made by an ex-commander-or even by an ex-cabinet minister.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
But would the Prime Minister be good enough to address his mind seriously to this question. Does he regard it as satisfactory
Supply-National Defence
that statements should 'be made to congressional committees in the United States by retiring commanders on the subject of the alleged shortage of ammunition without information being conveyed to this house in order to remove a possible misleading statement of this kind?
The Prime Minister; I do not think it would be a good thing if we were to let our procedure in this house be governed by investigations of congressional committees in the United States. I should have thought that the right hon. gentleman ought to be very careful when he pursues this line as he might be falling out with some of his colleagues below the gangway.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
Does not the right hon. gentleman understand that I am anxious not to fall out with anybody but if I had to choose between my hon. friends below the gangway and the Prime Minister I should prefer the right hon. gentleman because he is much easier to handle. Will he be good enough to make inquiries and to ascertain whether the statements by General Van Fleet are accurate? After all, we ought to be assured on a very important subject of this kind.
The Prime Minister: We have regular reports, and very close and intimate relations prevail between the British military representative and the commander in chief in Korea. I have no doubt that the reports we have received fully justify us in giving our full confidence to the character of the statements made. May I thank the right hon. gentleman for the compliment which he paid me and only express my regret that he should have thought it necessary to add any reservation.
On the same day the views of President Eisenhower were expressed, and they were quoted in the Washington Post of March 27. I read:
President Eisenhower said yesterday there is sufficient ammunition in Korea for present scale operations and then described the supply situation as perfectly sound under current circumstances. Across the Atlantic, Prime Minister Winston Churchill gave similar assurances to the House of Commons and an army spokesman said that shipments of some types of ammunition have been diverted to other areas because Far East pipe lines of such shells are now full.
The president was asked about the ammunition situation at his news conference. He said he had questioned the Pentagon about it and if there was any relation between the shortage and the loss of Baldy Ridge hill in Korea, given up by American troops yesterday after a heavy fight. The army chiefs assured him emphatically that ammunition was not a factor in the loss of the position, Mr. Eisenhower said. In fact, he added, the Far East command turned back a shipload of ammunition because the reserves of that particular type were so high they didn't want it.

What happened was that the British were in need of some 25-pounder shells at the beginning of the war in Korea and we sent them 200,000. That was our contribution to the commonwealth supply line. Shells for 25-pounders, some mortar bombs and small arms ammunition now come from British production. Ammunition for other weapons comes off the American supply line. We generally get the same treatment as anyone else. The situation was as I indicated in my statement in the house last December, and since then it has steadily improved.
The next reference with which I wish to deal is that made by the hon. member for Brandon with respect to welfare. I must say that I think an apology is owing to him for some delay in completing the answer to a return he asked for some time ago, but it required investigation and checking in both Korea and Germany. I have a number of quotations, extracts and so on and so forth which run directly contrary to some of those which have been used in the house, but I will not give them now. I should add, however, that it has been decided to institute a Canadian army welfare fund similar to the benevolent funds for the air force and navy for the purpose of extending benefits to serving personnel. That has been set up and a statement to that effect will go out tonight.
With regard to one or two other matters, the hon. member for Kootenay West and other hon. members have referred again to these global figures for items such as rugs, furniture and the like. speechtext: Yes, Mr. Chairman. Last year the committee on defence expenditure referred to a great many items and if they did not include rugs that was surely by way of oversight, because rugs were dealt with in the house, as I see by the statement made on November 27, 1952.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
Now, sir, hon. members of the opposition have on a good many occasions made sweeping statements about extravagance, waste and the like; and those usually take the form of stating a large figure: "They have spent $251,000 on landscape gardening; so much on ties", and so on. Those assertions are played up and made use of repeatedly, as if there was something wrong because the figures happen to be large. The figures happen

Supply-National Defence to be large because of the scale of the operations, and the place where these things can be looked into best has been and is, I suggest, before the committee on defence expenditure.
An illustration of this situation perhaps can be given in the simplest possible terms. Many hon. members of the opposition have made a good deal of the fact that we bought a lot of ties. We need 420,000 ties a year to supply each member of the armed forces who has to wear a tie with the minimum number required to equip him. You have to think in terms of that sum.
The Leader of the Opposition followed the hon. member for Calgary East by referring to some shortages in the equipment of the reserve forces. He described them as deplorable and likely to produce an attitude of frustration and so on. Well, we have some hundreds of units in the reserve force of the army and their effort is to do the best job they can-and a very good job they do, too. They are handicapped in that effort if they have more equipment than they need for the purposes of their training; so effort is constantly made by the reserve forces themselves to reduce the amount of their equipment to that which they need for training purposes.
In the question put by the Leader of the Opposition it would appear that he had in mind an artillery regiment. Indeed, it would look as if he were quoting from the same text that was referred to by the hon. member for Calgary East. As far back as last August information went out that the number of guns that would be available for the training of each artillery regiment would be reduced to the number they could usefully use. The distribution was put under the command of the general officer commanding. It was before the conference of defence associations at their meeting in Ottawa in January, 1953, and no complaint whatever was made about the result. Indeed, it appears to have been in accordance with their wishes. The general officers commanding and area commanders recently had their conference in Ottawa and the question was not raised. As far as one can see this was a thoroughly sensible course, in accordance with the wishes of the units.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Probably they asked for guns without breeches and breech rings, did they?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
With regard to the question of breech rings, in consequence of experience gained in Korea it was decided just before Christmas of this year to make modifications in the breech rings in order to ensure greater security, this despite the fact that 25-pounders have been in production and use for a number


of years. So the breech rings are being modified, and that modification will be completed before the coming training seasoip Had an accident occurred by reason of failure to carry out that modification, the necessity of which was borne in by experience in Korea, I am sure that hon. members opposite would have been the first to call this to our attention.
Now, sir, I think I have dealt with most of the points covered by hon. members opposite. If there are any that I have not covered I am sure they will be drawn to my attention and we can deal with them as we get into the detailed discussion of the estimates.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
Before we go into the discussion of the details, there is one question I should like to ask the minister, arising out of his observations. Just before the recess he referred to a statement I made yesterday with reference to the former destroyer
H.M.C.S. Algonquin, which I had said was being converted at the Yarrows yard in Esquimalt and was the only prototype of the new anti-submarine escort ships that have so far been commissioned. The minister said the Algonquin is not the prototype of the new anti-submarine escort vessel, but she is the first of our Tribal class destroyers to be modernized, equipped with new mess decks, bunks, new electronic fire control apparatus and the like. She is not one of the new anti-submarine escort vessels. I think I took down the minister's words correctly.
I based my statement on information which appeared in a magazine entitled Canadian Shipping and Marine Engineering News, March 1953, the Royal Canadian Navy issue, and particularly an article entitled "The Navy's Progress", by the Hon. Brooke Claxton, D.C.M.,	Q.C., Minister of National
Defence. In this article the minister said:
A prototype of Canada's new anti-submarine escort ships, the former destroyer H.M.C.S. Algonquin, was commissioned in February, and the job of converting another destroyer, H.M.C.S. Crescent, into a similar deadly foe of the submarine, was taken in hand.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I do submit that these are two diametrically opposed statements. On the one hand the minister says Algonquin is not the prototype of the new anti-submarine escort ships, and the month before he wrote an article in a trade magazine in which he said that she is the prototype of the new anti-submarine escort vessels. These conflicting statements only lead to confusion, not only confusion for members of the opposition who try to base their arguments on statements made by the minister, but also confusion in the minds of the public. I do not know which of these two exactly

opposite statements is correct, and I would ask the minister.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Convicted out of his own mouth.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Neither is correct.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: The titles of these ships, as the hon. member may know, change from time to time according to the type of description applied to them.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: They change every time the minister speaks.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Wait.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: The type of ship which we generally call the anti-submarine escort vessel is the new type which is being produced, the first of which is the St. Laurent, which was launched last year. The Tribal class destroyers are being reconverted for antisubmarine work, but they are not the antisubmarine escort ships.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Then the statement in this edition of Canadian Shipping of March, 1953, by the minister is incorrect.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to discuss not the details of the equipment but the broad question of organization. Before doing that, I should like to make one or two comments on the speech which the minister has just finished.
I was rather puzzled by the comments he made about Wing Commander Rohmer. It did not seem to me that it was important to know whether he was No. 286 on the list or whether he had a pleasant talk with Crawford Gordon, Jr., or whether he wrote a letter to Crawford Gordon, Jr., or whether he was the partner of a Conservative candidate and an active Liberal party worker in Toronto. I think the only thing that was important was whether or not what he said was true. I understand that what he said was exactly what the hon. member for Nanaimo said, and that it has not been either controverted or attempted to be controverted in any way.
The minister began by saying that this gentleman was an officer with a good record. But from that point on it seemed to me the disposition was rather to play him down. It will be a sorry day when we try to play down men who have the courage to say what they think. One of the troubles is that there are so few people who do have that courage.
I should like to draw attention to another thing. At the beginning of the minister's speech he referred to the fact that the Leader of the Opposition had expressed approval of what is called our No. 2 obligation, that is
Supply-National Defence the obligation to NATO and our obligations under the United Nations charter. I am quite satisfied that the Leader of the Opposition is ready to give credit where credit is due.
With regard to the other two points-No. 1, the defence of Canada against enemy attack, and No. 3, the organizations to build up strength in a total war-I confess I found myself very disappointed with the words which the minister used. Speaking of the Leader of the Opposition he said: "If he stays on that side of the house and we stay on this side, as we all expect will be the case for some time further,"-that was just thrown in-"it may be that he will be in a position next year or perhaps the following year to acknowledge that we have done equally well on the first and third points because we are just on the way to getting there."
I think the taxpayers will be disappointed at the fact that all the minister can say is "maybe next year or perhaps the following year." In that connection I wish to read from today's Ottawa Journal concerning the increasing futurity, we might say, of the progress that they are making in the Department of National Defence. Speaking of the white paper the Journal says:
We read them, anxious and eager to agree with Mr. Claxton that all is going well and that our billions of dollars of expenditure have brought us the utmost in defence security; but we cannot, no matter how we try.
One reason for our cautious approach to these white papers is Mr. Claxton's persistent use of the words "will be", his emphasis about the arms we are to have rather than the sabre in our national fist at the moment. For example, we have looked up the 1952-53 white paper and it said: "At present the fighter squadrons for this purpose (fighter defence of Canada) are equipped with Vampire and Mustang aircraft. These will be replaced by CF-lOO's as they become available. In addition, there are a number of squadrons equipped with F-86E's and designated for the NATO air force in Europe. In the meantime they are available for the defence of this continent.
The following year, in the 1953-54 white paper, I read the following from the white paper:
The first regular squadron, equipped with CF-100 all-weather, twin-engine, jet fighters, was recently formed and by the end of the fiscal year a number of these squadrons will be operating. Meanwhile, a number of squadrons of F-86E Sabres, destined as part of Canada's NATO air contribution, have been in Canada available for the defence of this continent. As the last of these are sent to Europe during the year, their places will be taken by squadrons of CF-lOO's. Reserve squadrons now equipped with Vampires and Mustangs will be re-equipped with CF-lOO's as these become available.
And the Journal goes on briefly:
So, apart from that one squadron with an unstated number of aircraft, the CF-lOO's are still

Supply-National Defence in the "will be" stage, and antiquated Vampires and Mustangs remain to be counted anlong the defenders of the nation in the case of a sudden attack.
I wish to direct the rest of my remarks to what I think may be called No. 3 of these objectives, although it affects them all. I refer to the objective of enabling us to mobilize our forces to meet an all-out attack. I wish to discuss that matter from the point of view of the whole organization of the Department of National Defence and its conjoint companies, defence production, defence construction and Central Mortgage and Housing.
I put it this way to you, Mr. Chairman. Two years ago or thereabouts we started on a huge new enterprise on which we have spent billions of dollars. In his speech the minister referred to the capital expenditure and put it at $2,767 million. Then the minister proceeded to talk with what seemed to me to be great satisfaction about the fact that we had managed to spend all this money. He told us that it involved hundreds of contracts. Actually it came to sound like a song of billions. But for the most part or indeed almost altogether it seemed that we were just listening to an outline of huge expenditures.
For example, the minister compared it with the expenditures of the Canadian National Railways. He said that in 25 years the Canadian National Railways had managed to spend only $1,341 million; and I presume this is on capital account. He pointed out, apparently with pride, that in two and a half years our defence program has managed to spend more than twice as much as this. Then he gave us an illustration of a private corporation. He gave as an illustration the Shawinigan company which I think he said in 50 years had spent something like $335 million, although I am not quite sure about that figure.
What I felt was that all these figures were splendidly irrelevant. They seemed to me to have nothing to do with the case. To me the whole point is to know not whether we spent all this money-I have no doubt that we did-but whether we did so effectively. From listening to the minister, as far as I could see one was almost supposed to assume that we had spent this money effectively. From the fact that we had been able to enter into all these contracts and have everything done according to legal form by all the various companies, including defence construction, defence production, Central Mortgage and Housing and national defence-I find it difficult to remember all the names-we were


supposed to assume that that in itself was a great achievement.
Then we have had criticisms in this debate. We have had criticisms that have been referred to tonight. I do not propose to take the time of the committee to refer to them. Those gentlemen who have made their criticisms and who have been answered-and in my opinion very ineffectively-will be prepared to say whatever further needs to be said on those subjects. I come back to the question of organization.
Many months ago, indeed I think I may say years ago, when this thing first came up, we on this side felt that this was a tremendous job; and I think sincerely enough we tried to press that view on those across the gangway. It seemed to us-and I have never been able to get away from that feeling-that the matter was taken too lightly. I myself asked a question in the house on May 24, 1951. I tried to stress as best I could what seemed to me to be the magnitude and the complexity of this job, and I asked whether any expert assistance was being sought. I asked whether the government was seeking in any way to get assistance, and the answer I got was this:
it-
That is the department.
-is set up in accordance with the practice which has obtained in the Department of National Defence over the years. There has not been much change. We have to do a job, and we do it.
I might point out, too, that there was a slight inaccuracy in that statement of the minister because my understanding is that during the war years Colonel Ralston did in fact bring in several top-ranking businessmen to assist him, one of them being Mr. Currie with whose name we are all so familiar. Hence in fact it was not just the department itself that he relied on. He went outside for assistance.
We know that there are people who specialize in organization and who have useful help which they can give if they are asked for it. Of course it is always arguable that there are men who do not need to be trained in administration, that there are men of genius who seem to be able to do things without the training and experience that ordinary men need; and it was always arguable that we might have found that * these men were in the Department of National Defence. So far as I can see, that assumption was made, namely that without any outside assistance and without any outside advice they had succeeded in mastering this tremendous job. As a matter of fact, I was assured by the department that these efficiency companies

really were not competent to assist large organizations, that they could assist only the small fry. That was just a complete misunderstanding of the assistance that was available if it had been sought.
Yesterday the minister made a great point of telling us that he had had few letters of complaint. He said you could count them on two hands. I did not take much stock in that answer. The complaints would have to come mainly from two sources. The first source would be somebody in the services. I do not need to tell you, Mr. Chairman, that people in the services are not going to be very ready to write letters of complaint to the minister. That would be a rather unusual thing to do. Then the second source would be people who are doing business with the government; and I do not think they would be very free in writing letters of criticism either. They want to do business with the government, not to criticize them. I am therefore not at all impressed by that test which the minister applied.
We in the opposition have tried to make effective criticisms. We have not done it to our own liking; but I leave the matter to anyone who looks at the thing in a detached way. It is extremely difficult to drive your criticisms home if you have no means of making an independent examination and if you are left entirely to departmental officials who, however competent they are and however desirous they are of doing the right ' thing, have got to take the departmental line. How could they do anything else? They are in a department and they must take that line. Let us be realistic about the thing.
So things went along, Mr. Chairman, and we were uneasy. I think many people were uneasy. Then something more than a year ago an event took place which perhaps is an illustration of the old hymn that "God moves in a mysterious way"; because an anonymous letter really touched off something. There was an anonymous letter which indicated that all was not well at Petawawa; and as a result of this letter the minister took the entirely proper and wise action of appointing Mr. Currie to make an investigation, which he did.
We know about the investigation. It was discussed in the house. But once the report was brought in, it did not seem to attract much favour among the ministers. Mr. Currie suddenly descended from the heights which he had occupied, and we suddenly found that this idol, in the eyes of the ministers, had feet of clay.
I must say that the Minister of Trade and Commerce made a very gallant attempt to 68108-249

He was paying his tribute to the opposition, and in the midst of it he said this:
Opposition parties will say: "What about the Currie report? They are all we need to prove our charges." What are the tacts?
And then the minister went on:
Mr. Currie in his report did not find any waste or inefficiency, nor does he claim to have found any. It was the Minister of National Defence who discovered irregularities in the army works service at Petawawa.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce was not quite fair to the anonymous letter, but we will pass that. I continue:
It was he who brought to justice those who conspired together to steal a few thousand of dollars worth of public property, and those who personally profited through some of the operations of the army works company at Petawawa camp. You will I hope realize, Mr. Chairman, that what I have read would seem to indicate that the Currie report, far from being critical of the Department of National Defence, was almost a eulogy. The minister I am sure will not misunderstand it if I say I really think that is one of the most splendid instances of sublime arrogance that I have ever seen. I do not know how the minister got into that frame of mind. The rest of us all thought this report was a criticism. The minister says it is not a criticism. It carried me back to a thing I never could understand when I went to school. It was a thing called a syllogism, a form of reasoning that was always over my head.

I think the ordinary person, not one of those people who are living in this rarefied atmosphere, but just the ordinary Joe, as we call him, would think that it would be reasonable when you found a state of gross-what shall we say- gross irregularity, gross inefficiency in the department, an attempt would be made to extend the examination. I would say that anyone outside of a kindergarten, or even inside a kindergarten, would think that was reasonable. And of course we all know that in a private business, if a department was found to be ineffective or inefficient and the manager did not move to have the whole business investigated, he would get the sack. It is just as simple as that. But to this government nothing is impossible, nothing unreasonable is impossible, and so there has been no inquiry. It was voted down.
I can only imagine the government hopes that memories are very short. It is their hope that before the 10th day of August, that magic date which is being bandied about by the Citizen and in other places, this will be forgotten.
I do want to make one reference to the Currie report, because in addition to the blistering criticism of the department's administration, Mr. Currie makes one statement which I think is so far-reaching and goes so much to the root of the matter that I want to read it, and I want to support it a little later on; and I do hope that it will be in order. I am watching awfully carefully, Mr. Chairman. At page 717 of Hansard of December last Mr. Currie, after his various detailed criticisms of what he found, goes on to what seems to me to be the basic criticism that he makes, which goes to the
[Mr. Macdonnell (Greenwood) .1

very root of the matter and which personally I find very convincing, because I think it would be nothing short of a miracle if this organization could have been licked into satisfactory shape just by a sort of hit-or-miss method, and I have never been able to discover any other which has been used. This is what Mr. Currie says:
What is needed now is the creation of a system-
I want to repeat that:
What is needed now is the creation of a system-
It is not a modification or a little change here and there, but the creation of a system. -designed to fit the economic and efficient administration of a large and long-sustained preparedness program inside a national economy operating at full blast.
Now, Mr. Chairman, there you see a man who knows his onions. There is a man who knows something about the economy and what fitting this into the economy means, because he is at once a distinguished businessman and a distinguished public servant. They could not have found a man better qualified. The minister did a great public service when he got Mr. Currie to go into this a year ago. The only trouble is, having got him, and having got the medicine, they would not take it. I continue:-

I have no intention of supporting that thesis because I have not given the matter enough thought. I am raising this only to show that this question of organization is exercising other people, and to show that there is a great disturbance of minds as to whether or not our organization is sound. I should like to read from another of these articles where reference is made to the hon. member for Nanaimo and a reference by him to the National Defence Act which was approved in 1950. This article reads:
When the act was referred to a special committee of the House of Commons, General G. R. Pearkes, V.C., the Progressive Conservative for Nanaimo, commented on the wide powers it gave to the chief of the general staff.
I might interject here to say that the thesis of this writer, as far as I can make it out, is that the army chiefs have been given too much power. I continue to quote from the article which is quoting the hon. member for Nanaimo:
"Mr. Chairman, I do not know whether the committee is aware of the fact, but I think there is a bigger change here in so far as the army and the general administration of the staff are concerned than in any other section of the act. Here you are changing the whole system of the staff control of the army.
In the past you have had the general staff represented by the chief of the general staff, who has had the responsibility of co-ordinating the work of the other branches of the staff, the adjutant-general, the quartermaster-general and the master-general of ordnance.
Here you are placing the chief of the general staff in a position senior to the heads of the other branches, and that is really a major change which is going back almost to the system which was in vogue in 1904, when you had a commander-inchief of the army.
I shall go on now to make a few further brief remarks. I come back to the words used by Mr. Currie, "the creation of a system". This report was made by a competent man. Of course we thought that the inquiry should be extended, but it was not. I am not going to say anything about that, Mr. Chairman, because I see you shaking your head at me. But I think we might have expected that there would have been some indication in the minister's speech that somewhere there had been a stirring of the waters, that something was going to be done, that there was not complete satisfaction with the present situation. However, I could not detect anything of that kind in the minister's speech.

I want to be fair in this and say that we have been given quite a lot of information; but the question is, what kind of information? When I say "screened" I am not suggesting anything sinister-I want to be fair to the situation; but it is not the kind of information you get when you send in your own representative, when you send in an independent person to inspect. It is suggested to me that it is edited information. In one sense it is.
I have talked long enough and you have been most patient with me, for which I am grateful. I just want to say that the situation is unsatisfactory. It is perfectly clear that at the moment the defence of Canada is in a most unsatisfactory state. The minister used a phrase which at one time was used a great deal, that the sound thing is to defend your country as far away from your country as possible. But that remark would be valid only before the days of global aircraft. I am not sure, but I think that phrase was used first of all by the Australians in Africa, who said that they went to Africa because they preferred to defend Australia there.
As the hon. member for Nanaimo said, what is the use of saying that, unless you can get the enemy to agree to fight it out, say, in the Falkland islands? We know that at the present time the situation is unsatisfactory and there is no use of having any make-up about it. I can only hope that as a result of this debate and other means of enlightenment the people of Canada will wake up to the situation. If they do I am quite sure they will find it to be most unsatisfactory.

When I first knew Vice-Admiral Mainguy in St. John's, Newfoundland, in the last war he was then known as Captain D, and he was the person responsible for the establishment of what has become in naval circles, and almost internationally, a very well known place, the Crows' Nest in St. John's, Newfoundland. St. John's, Newfoundland, was indeed a very honoured place in those days because of the great number of ships that called there and because of the very real pleasure the navy extended to the residents of St. John's which they were happy to reciprocate in kind.

A good deal has been said and written during the past few years on the subject of the R.C.N.'s chief potential antagonist, the modern submarine, but the fact remains that only a few have any clear understanding of its real, and considerable, destructive power. This should be as well known to every Canadian as it is to those who might seek to use it against us, for it is among the gravest threats that we may have to face as a nation should we become involved in yet another great destructive war.
In appearance the post-war model submarine is not vastly different from its sufficiently troublesome predecessors. In performance it is in many respects an entirely different vessel, with some rather alarming characteristics and possibilities. In the first place, its underwater speed is approximately double that which could be attained by the U-boats of the second world war. Secondly, the depth to which the submarine can dive is steadily increasing. This makes it harder to detect and increases its chances of escape even if detected.
Then he talks about the German apparatus which we knew as the snorkel but which he calls the "snort". He says that with the snort installed this submarine of the modern age can now stay down for a matter of weeks. He says that the modern submarine has a range of 5,000 miles, and carries torpedoes whose range may now be calculated in miles and which are equipped with targetfinding devices which have increased their effectiveness most seriously. He goes on and enlarges upon the fact that the submarine with its new potential killing apparatus is an infinitely more dangerous weapon than ever before. Then he says:
The submarine Is thus faster, harder to catch, harder to kill and possessed of greater destructive power than at any time in the past. What is more, it can be built in quantity. The U.S.S.R. has today some five or six times as many submarines as the Germans had in 1939, and is certainly building many more of advanced types. The present fleet is actually about the size of that possessed by Germany at the zenith of success in the last war. There is every indication that it will continue to grow.
I am by no means competent to evaluate properly the findings of the chief of the naval staff except as an ordinary common-sense individual reading common-sense language. The Minister of Fisheries may say that I cannot write too well, but I can read better than I can write.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Well, I have a question of privilege.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: You are getting a lot of help.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: My question of privilege is that we are discussing here the estimates of the Department of National Defence. It is my understanding that, according to the rules of the house, the minister is bound to answer questions which are put to him.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: That is a perfectly good question of privilege.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I want to listen to the hon. member for St. John's East, but the hon. member for Calgary East and the hon. member for Kamloops prevent me from listening to him.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
Someone suggests that time will be killed. Perhaps I should kill it myself and therefore settle the argument.
The point I want to bring forward is that last year and two years ago when we studied the estimates of the Department of National Defence there was an agreed procedure, which we are following this year. It is that first of all we have a general policy discussion and, as soon as that is over, we carry on with the question and answer period. I think we are still at the general policy discussion period.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: May I help the hon. member for St. John's East out of his difficulty by taking up the remaining time-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: No, no, no, Mr. Chairman.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Held over.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: The date in the white paper for ships and such matters is up to February 28, or some date in February. The paper was set up in proof form but dates and figures were changed as they came in, particularly regarding manpower. Subsequent to the insertion of the figure of two ships launched, shown there as at the month of February, there was one ship launched. Hence my statement today. Admiral Mainguy's statement in the publication from which you are reading, and the statement in the white paper are all correct.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Mr. Chairman-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: May I ask the Minister of National Defence not to imply-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: -that perhaps the hon. member for St. John's East had in his mind to kill time. Also, I would not want anything I said myself, when I made a remark in a light vein, to be construed to the effect that the hon. member was trying to kill time.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: The clock has let you all out.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Before you call it ten o'clock, I think the minister should withdraw that remark.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
You will agree, sir, that it is easier to kill time than it is to kill the minister.
Supply-National Defence

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I would like the minister to withdraw the remark that the hon. member was killing time.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I am glad to see that at this closing hour hon. members are still in a very good mood. I might tell the hon. member for Calgary East that under the rules the implication which was perhaps in the minister's remark is not offensive and I do not think I should ask him to withdraw. Might I make the suggestion that no implication should be left of accusing an hon. member of trying to kill time. The minister has nodded his head in agreement with me. That nod will not appear on Hansard but my explanations will clear up the situation, and I think that will satisfy the hon. member.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
May I make a suggestion? I realize that the minister has been under a bit of cross-heckling today, if you will, and I am quite certain that he did not mean the remark he made. Even if he did it would be understandable. I was really not trying to kill time, but I was pressing the point I was trying to make, and I will make it tomorrow, maybe.
Item stands.
Progress reported.

maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, tomorrow we shall take up the second reading of Bill No. 334, an act to provide for the superannuation of persons employed in the public service of Canada. After second reading this bill will be referred immediately to the committee on banking and commerce. I should like to see the bill reach that stage, because the Minister of Finance will be absent for a week and we shall have time to make a serious study of this bill in the committee. Then we shall take up the estimates of national defence and trade and commerce.

maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: In that order?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: In that order.
At ten o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Thursday, April 16, 1953
